lessons.title: Früher musste ich, früher wollte ich: müssen and wollen in the past
lessons.goal: Say 3 or 4 sentences about what you had to do and wanted to do in primary school, using musste and wollte.

grammar.point: müssen and wollen have a one-word past: ich musste, du musstest, wir mussten; ich wollte, du wolltest, wir wollten. The modal is in part 2 and the second verb stays in the infinitive at the end.
grammar.oneLine: Früher musste ich früh aufstehen. Past modal in part 2, infinitive last.

mistake.why: After a time word such as früher, the verb is still part 2. The subject ich goes behind the modal, and aufstehen stays at the end.

terms.meaning: the one-word past, for example war, hatte, musste. Also called simple past.
the basic form of a verb, for example aufstehen
a helper verb such as müssen or wollen that sits in part 2 while the other verb goes to the end

cards.title: Before we start: what was school like for you?
cards.body: Welcome to A2, chapter 2: Nach der Schulzeit. In three lessons you talk about your school days, then about jobs and training. Today you learn to say what you had to do and what you wanted to do back then. People ask this all the time: Wie war deine Schulzeit?
steps: You already know: ich muss, ich will, and the second verb at the end, from A1. You also know war and hatte.
New today: the one-word past of müssen and wollen: ich musste, ich wollte. The second verb still waits at the end.
By the end you can: tell 3 or 4 sentences about what you had to do and wanted to do in primary school.

examples.en: I have to get up early.
examples.why: You know this: modal in part 2, infinitive at the end.

examples.en: Earlier I had to get up early.
examples.why: New today: musste is the past of muss. The infinitive is still at the end.

cards.more: Think of a time machine. Today the sentence stays the same, only the modal verb gets a ticket to the past. Ich muss becomes ich musste. Ich will becomes ich wollte. Everything else stays where it was: the modal is in seat 2 and the second verb waits in the last seat. You only need one new word at the start to say when it was: früher, which means earlier. That is all. Small change, big result: now you can talk about your childhood.

cards.title: War and hatte: the short past you already know
cards.body: Germans use war and hatte for sein and haben in the past, even when they talk. Früher war ich klein. This is the model for today: one short word, no helper verb. The modals müssen and wollen work the same way.

examples.en: Earlier I was small.

examples.de: In der Grundschule hatte ich viel Zeit.
examples.en: In primary school I had a lot of time.

examples.de: Wir waren oft auf dem Schulhof.
examples.en: We were often on the school yard.

cards.lead: In the introduction you saw ich musste as a goal. On this card: war and hatte, the short past of sein and haben. They are the model for the modals on the next cards.

deeper.text: Präteritum is the grammar name for this one-word past. Ich war and er war look the same, and so do ich hatte and sie hatte. For most verbs people use the Perfekt when they speak, but war, hatte and the modals keep the short form, even in a chat. You see this rule again on every card today.

example.en: My school time was nice.

cards.more: Imagine two small words that live in the past: war and hatte. They are tiny and everybody uses them, in books and in the kitchen. Ich bin müde today, ich war müde yesterday. Ich habe Zeit today, ich hatte Zeit yesterday. Step 1: say the present. Step 2: swap it for the past word. Step 3: keep the rest. The modals will join this little family in a moment.

cards.title: müssen in the past: musste
cards.body: To say had to, make müssen one short word: ich musste. The umlaut ü disappears and -te is added. After that the endings look like war and hatte: du musstest, wir mussten, ihr musstet.

examples.en: I had to get up early.

examples.de: Mira musste um sieben Uhr in der Schule sein.
examples.en: Mira had to be at school at seven.
We had to do homework.

cards.lead: You saw that war and hatte are one short word. On this card: müssen becomes musste, so you can say what you had to do when you were a child.

deeper.text: The modal ends in -te, and that -te is the sign of the past, like a small flag. The ü of müssen is gone because the past does not use an umlaut here. Ich and er/sie/es are always the same: ich musste, sie musste. Du gets -st, and wir and sie/Sie get -n: du musstest, wir mussten. Check the table and say it aloud.

example.en: You had to be quiet.

cards.more: Think of müssen as a word with a hat, the umlaut. In the past the hat falls off: müssen becomes muss. Then you give the word a past flag: -te. So you get musste. Step 1: müssen. Step 2: take off the hat: muss-. Step 3: add the flag: musste. Step 4: add the person ending if needed: musstest, mussten. Ich and sie share the same word, easy. Extra example: Ben musste lange warten.
steps: 1 Start with müssen.
2 Drop the umlaut: muss-.
3 Add the past flag: musste.
4 Add the person ending: du musstest, wir mussten.

cards.title: wollen in the past: wollte
cards.body: To say wanted to, do the same with wollen: ich wollte. There is no umlaut to drop. Add -te to the stem woll- and then the person ending: du wolltest, wir wollten, ihr wolltet.

examples.en: Ben did not want to get up.

examples.de: Wir wollten auf dem Schulhof spielen.
examples.en: We wanted to play on the school yard.
I wanted to eat a snack.

cards.lead: Now you can say what you had to do. On this card: wollen becomes wollte, so you can also say what you wanted to do or did not want to do.

deeper.text: Wollen is simpler than müssen because it has no umlaut. The pattern is stem + -te + person ending, and it is the same for every modal today. If you can say musste, you can say wollte. Ich and er/sie/es are again identical. The ending -st for du and -n for wir and sie/Sie show up in every row.

example.en: You did not want to go.

cards.more: Wollen is the easy one. Take the stem woll- and add the past flag -te: wollte. Step 1: wollen. Step 2: woll-. Step 3: woll- + te = wollte. Step 4: add the person ending when you need it: du wolltest, wir wollten. Picture a child who does not want to get up: Ich wollte nicht aufstehen. Same shape as musste. Extra example: Anna wollte spielen.
steps: 1 Start with wollen.
2 Take the stem: woll-.
3 Add the past flag: wollte.
4 Add the person ending: du wolltest, wir wollten.

cards.title: The second verb goes to the end
cards.body: With a modal in the past, the order is the same as in the present. The modal is in part 2. The second verb stays in the infinitive and waits at the end. Separable verbs stay in one piece: aufstehen, abholen, mitbringen.

examples.en: My father wanted to pick me up.
examples.why: abholen stays whole at the end.

examples.en: Anna had to bring her snack.
examples.why: mitbringen stays whole at the end.

examples.en: Leon wanted to pick Ben up.
examples.why: The modal is part 2, the infinitive is last.

cards.lead: You can build musste and wollte. On this card: where the second verb goes, the infinitive at the end, even for verbs like aufstehen and abholen that you know as split verbs.

deeper.text: In the present, split verbs break apart: ich stehe auf. With a modal this does not happen. The modal takes part 2, and the other verb does not move: ich musste aufstehen. Everything in the middle, such as früh or mich, sits between the two verbs. The sentence is like a bracket: modal on the left, infinitive on the right.

example.en: I had to get up early.

cards.more: Imagine a sentence as a sandwich. The modal is the left slice of bread, the infinitive is the right slice. Everything else goes in between, like cheese: früh, mich, Hausaufgaben. The right slice never splits, so aufstehen stays one word. Step 1: put the modal in seat 2. Step 2: put the extra pieces in the middle. Step 3: put the infinitive last. Extra example: Wir wollten Ben mitbringen.

cards.title: Questions and nicht
cards.body: Questions work like in the present. For a yes/no question the modal comes first: Musstest du …? With a question word, it is part 2: Warum wolltest du …? Ich musste nicht means I did not have to.

examples.en: Did you have to do homework?
examples.why: Yes/no question: the modal is first.

examples.en: Why did you not want to go?
examples.why: Question word first, modal in part 2.

examples.en: I did not have to.

cards.lead: You know where the verbs go. On this card: asking questions in the past, so you can ask a friend what they had to do or did not want to do, and answer with ja or nein.

deeper.text: In a statement the modal is in part 2. In a yes/no question it moves to the front and the subject follows it. After a question word such as warum, the modal is again in part 2. For short answers use ja and nein plus the modal alone: Ja, ich musste. Nein, ich musste nicht. You can drop the second verb because everybody knows it.

example.en: Did you not want to play?

cards.more: A question is just a statement with a small shuffle. In a statement the modal is in seat 2. In a yes/no question it jumps to seat 1: Musstest du? With warum in seat 1, the modal stays in seat 2: Warum wolltest du? For the answer, you only say ja or nein and the modal. Ja, ich musste. Nein, ich musste nicht. That is enough, nobody needs the rest.

rows: Ja, ich musste. / Nein, ich musste nicht.

cards.title: Time chunks: früher, damals, in der Grundschule
cards.body: A story about the past needs time words. They usually come first in the sentence, and then the verb stays in part 2. Learn them as chunks: früher, damals, in der Grundschule, mit sechs Jahren.

examples.en: Earlier I had to get up early.
examples.why: Früher is part 1, musste is part 2.

examples.en: Back then I only wanted to play.

examples.de: Mit sechs Jahren musste ich zur Schule gehen.
examples.en: At six I had to go to school.
examples.why: Time chunk first, then the modal.

cards.lead: You can ask and answer. On this card: four time chunks that tell the listener when something happened, so your stories about the past sound real.

deeper.text: Früher means earlier, damals means back then, and in der Grundschule means in primary school. All of them are time words, so they take part 1 and push the subject behind the modal. Mit sechs Jahren is one chunk: at the age of six. Do not worry about why it ends in -en, just learn the whole piece.

example.de: In der Grundschule hatte ich viel Zeit.
example.en: In primary school I had a lot of time.

cards.more: Time words are signposts. Früher says: this is the past, listen. Damals says: back then. When one signpost stands in seat 1, the modal stays in seat 2 and the subject ich moves behind it. Step 1: choose a signpost. Step 2: put the modal next. Step 3: put ich after it. Step 4: finish with the second verb. Extra example: Damals musste ich leise sein.

cards.title: Mira's school morning
cards.body: Here is Mira's school morning in five sentences. Read them aloud and find the modal in each one. The modal is always in part 2, and the second verb waits at the end. Then tell your own school morning in the same way.

examples.de: Früher musste ich um sechs Uhr aufstehen.
examples.en: Earlier I had to get up at six.
examples.why: Time chunk first, modal in part 2.

examples.en: I had to bring my snack.
examples.why: The second verb is at the end.

examples.de: In der Klasse wollte ich immer mit Anna lernen.
examples.en: In class I always wanted to study with Anna.

cards.lead: You now have all the pieces. On this last card, read them together in a short story, so you can see how musste, wollte and war fit into real sentences about the past.

deeper.text: In Germany the first school day is a big event, the Einschulung. Children get a Schultüte, a big paper cone with sweets and small gifts. Many parents take photos of this day. Your own story does not need to be that big. Two or three sentences with früher or damals, a modal and an infinitive at the end are a good start.

example.en: The way to school was long.

cards.more: A story is only a row of short sentences, each one built like a sandwich: signpost, modal, middle, infinitive. Read the five sentences slowly. Step 1: find the time chunk. Step 2: find the modal. Step 3: find the infinitive at the end. Step 4: say the sentence again without looking. After five times you will feel the rhythm. Then make one sentence about you.
steps: Früher musste ich um sechs Uhr aufstehen.
Ich wollte nicht aufstehen, aber ich musste.
Ich musste mein Pausenbrot mitbringen.
Der Schulweg war lang, aber ich hatte immer Zeit.
In der Klasse wollte ich immer mit Anna lernen.

lessons.title: Ich konnte, ich durfte: können and dürfen in the past
lessons.goal: Say what you could do and what you were allowed to do (or not) at school, using konnte and durfte.

grammar.point: können and dürfen have a one-word past: ich konnte, du konntest, wir konnten; ich durfte, du durftest, wir durften. The dots disappear. Konnte nicht means a skill is missing, durfte nicht means a rule forbids it.
grammar.oneLine: Ich konnte schwimmen. Ich durfte nicht laut sein. No dots, then -te.

mistake.why: The dots on ö disappear, but the letter becomes o, not a. So können gives konnte, and the second verb stays at the end.

terms.meaning: something you are able to do, said with können: Ich konnte schwimmen.
something you are allowed to do, said with dürfen: Ich durfte spielen.
the two dots on a, o or u: ä, ö, ü. The modals lose them in the past.

cards.title: Before we start: could and was allowed to
cards.body: When grown-ups talk about school days, two questions come up all the time: What could you do? What were you not allowed to do? Today you learn both in the past: Ich konnte schwimmen. Ich durfte nicht laut sein.
steps: You already know: ich kann and ich darf from A1, and from lesson 1 the past forms musste and wollte.
New today: the one-word past of können and dürfen: ich konnte, ich durfte. The second verb still waits at the end.
By the end you can: say 3 or 4 sentences about what you could do and what you were not allowed to do at school.

examples.en: I can swim.
examples.why: You know this: modal in part 2, infinitive at the end.

examples.de: Mit fünf Jahren konnte ich schon schwimmen.
examples.en: At five years old I could already swim.
examples.why: New today: konnte is the past of kann.

cards.more: Remember the time machine from lesson 1? Two more passengers get on today. Ich kann becomes ich konnte. Ich darf becomes ich durfte. Everything else stays the same: the modal sits in seat 2 and the second verb waits in the last seat. Können means to be able to. Dürfen means to be allowed to. When you were small, you could do some things, like swim, and some things were not allowed, like staying up late. Same machine, two new tickets.

cards.title: müssen and wollen: the pattern so far
cards.body: In lesson 1 you made müssen and wollen into one short word: musste, wollte. The pattern is always the same: take the stem, drop the two dots if there are any, add -te. Today können and dürfen join. See the two empty rows in the table.

examples.en: I had to get up early.
We wanted to play.
Earlier I had to be quiet.
examples.why: Time word first, modal in part 2.

cards.lead: Lesson 1 gave you musste and wollte. This card puts them side by side so you can spot the pattern, before können and dürfen join them on the next cards.

deeper.text: The ending -te is the sign of the past. With it, ich and er/sie/es become the same word: ich musste, sie musste. In the present, modals already do this (ich muss, sie muss). After the -te the person endings are simple: nothing for ich and er/sie/es, -st for du, -n for wir and sie/Sie, -t for ihr.

example.en: Mira did not want to study.

cards.more: Think of a recipe card with two spaces left blank. Müssen and wollen are already filled in: musste, wollte. The recipe is always the same. Step 1: take the stem. Step 2: if the vowel has two dots, take them off. Step 3: add -te. Step 4: add the person ending if you need one. Now the two blank spaces are waiting for können and dürfen. Try to guess them in your head before the next card.
steps: 1 Take the stem.
2 Drop the two dots if there are any.
3 Add the past flag -te.
4 Add the person ending: du -st, wir -n, ihr -t.

cards.title: können in the past: konnte
cards.body: To say could, make können one short word: ich konnte. The two dots on the ö disappear, so ö becomes o, and then -te is added. The endings are the same as before: du konntest, wir konnten, ihr konntet.

examples.en: I could read early.
examples.why: ich konnte: ö becomes o, then -te.

examples.en: Ben could not swim well.

examples.de: Mit sechs Jahren konnte Anna schon Fahrrad fahren.
examples.en: At six years old Anna could already ride a bike.
examples.why: Time chunk first, modal in part 2.

cards.lead: You saw the pattern for musste and wollte. Now können joins it, so you can say what you were able to do back then, like swimming or reading.

deeper.text: Können can also mean to know a skill or a language: Ich kann Englisch. In the past it works the same: Ich konnte Englisch. Watch the spelling: the vowel in konnte is o, never a. A form with a, kannte, is a different word with a different meaning. Say konnte aloud and keep the o short.

example.de: Du konntest damals schon Gitarre spielen.
example.en: Back then you could already play the guitar.

cards.more: Können wears two dots on the ö, like a hat. In the past the hat falls off and the letter changes shape: ö becomes o. Step 1: start with können. Step 2: take off the hat, so ö becomes o: konn-. Step 3: add the past flag -te: konnte. Step 4: add the person ending if you need one: du konntest, wir konnten. Extra example: Ich konnte nicht schlafen. Careful: it is konnte, not kannte.
steps: 1 Start with können.
2 ö becomes o: konn-.
3 Add the past flag: konnte.
4 Add the person ending: du konntest, wir konnten.

cards.title: dürfen in the past: durfte
cards.body: Dürfen means to be allowed to. Do the same as before: ü loses its dots and becomes u, then add -te: ich durfte. So you get du durftest, wir durften, ihr durftet. With nicht, durfte nicht means it was forbidden.

examples.en: I was not allowed to be loud.
examples.why: ich durfte: ü becomes u, then -te.

examples.de: Wir durften auf dem Schulhof Fußball spielen.
examples.en: We were allowed to play football on the school yard.
Leon was not allowed to watch TV in the evening.

cards.lead: You can now say what you were able to do. This card does the same for what you were allowed to do, because rules are a big part of every school memory.

deeper.text: In the present, dürfen with nicht means not allowed: Ich darf nicht rauchen. The past works the same way: Ich durfte nicht rauchen. Do not translate dürfen word for word with may or must not. Think allowed to. Notice also that durfte has a u, just like dürfen.

example.en: We were not allowed to come late.

cards.more: Dürfen also wears a hat, the two dots on the ü. In the past the hat falls off: ü becomes u. Step 1: start with dürfen. Step 2: take off the hat: durf-. Step 3: add the past flag: durfte. Step 4: add the person ending if you need one: du durftest, wir durften. Picture a child at the pool with a red sign: Ich durfte nicht ins Wasser. That is a rule, not a skill. Extra example: Ben durfte nicht warten.
steps: 1 Start with dürfen.
2 ü becomes u: durf-.
3 Add the past flag: durfte.
4 Add the person ending: du durftest, wir durften.

cards.title: All four together: müssen, wollen, können, dürfen
cards.body: Here are four modals in the past side by side. Three rules cover all of them: the dots disappear, the ending -te is added, and ich and er/sie/es are the same word. Learn the table by saying it aloud, row by row.

examples.de: Ich musste leise sein, aber ich wollte laut sein.
examples.en: I had to be quiet, but I wanted to be loud.

examples.de: Ben konnte schwimmen, aber er durfte nicht allein gehen.
examples.en: Ben could swim, but he was not allowed to go alone.
examples.why: Ability and rule in one sentence.

examples.de: Wir wollten draußen spielen, aber wir mussten lernen.
examples.en: We wanted to play outside, but we had to study.
examples.why: Each part has its modal in part 2.

cards.lead: You know four forms now. This card puts all four in one table, so you can see the pattern and say the whole family without stopping to think.

deeper.text: Ich and er/sie/es never differ in the past, and wir and sie/Sie never differ either. That means very few endings are left to learn: nothing for ich and er/sie/es, -st for du, -n for wir and sie/Sie, -t for ihr. Wollen is the only one of the four without dots, so it only gets -te. Sollen and mögen come in lesson 3.

example.de: Ihr wolltet spielen, aber ihr musstet lernen.
example.en: You wanted to play, but you had to study.

cards.more: Imagine four friends in a row, each with a past flag. Müssen carries musste, wollen carries wollte, können carries konnte, dürfen carries durfte. They share three habits. Habit 1: no dots. Habit 2: -te. Habit 3: ich and er/sie/es are twins. Say one row at a time: ich musste, wollte, konnte, durfte. Then the next row. After one round aloud you know the whole table.

cards.title: School rules back then: durfte nicht or musste?
cards.body: At school there were rules: things you had to do and things you were not allowed to do. Wir mussten leise sein. Wir durften im Unterricht nicht essen. Careful: durfte nicht means forbidden. It is not the same as musste nicht.

examples.de: Wir durften im Unterricht nicht essen.
examples.en: We were not allowed to eat in class.
examples.why: A rule that forbids: durfte nicht.

examples.en: We had to be quiet.

examples.de: Auf dem Schulhof durften wir laut sein.
examples.en: On the school yard we were allowed to be loud.

cards.lead: You can say what you could do and what you were allowed to do. This card shows how to talk about school rules, and how one small word, nicht, changes the meaning.

deeper.text: The word nicht changes the message in a surprising way. Ich musste nicht means I did not have to (it was not a duty). Ich durfte nicht means I was not allowed (it was forbidden). Learn them as two different messages. When a rule forbids something, always say durfte nicht.

example.en: We did not have to wait.

cards.more: Picture a traffic light. Red means stop: Ich durfte nicht. That is a rule against doing it. Blue means go, if you want: Ich musste nicht. Nobody forced me. And a bridge that is too high for you is a skill problem: Ich konnte nicht. Step 1: ask yourself who decides. Step 2: pick the modal. Step 3: add nicht. Extra example: Wir durften nicht rennen.

rows: I was not able to swim.
I was not allowed to swim.
I did not have to swim.

cards.title: Questions and short answers
cards.body: A question with a modal starts with the modal: Konntest du schon schwimmen? A short answer uses only the modal: Ja, ich konnte. Nein, ich konnte nicht. With a question word, the modal is still part 2: Was durftest du nicht machen?

examples.en: Could you swim already?
Were you allowed to eat in class?
What were you not allowed to do?

cards.lead: You can describe rules and abilities. This card turns them into questions and short answers, so you can ask a friend about their school days and answer quickly.

deeper.text: Du asks one person, ihr asks a group: Konntest du ...? Konntet ihr ...? Durftet ihr ...? In a short answer you may leave out the second verb, because everyone knows what you mean. In a longer answer you can add it again: Ja, ich konnte schwimmen.

example.en: Could you already read back then?

cards.more: A short answer is a ping-pong ball: the question flies over with the modal, and you hit the same modal back. Konntest du schwimmen? Ja, ich konnte. Durftet ihr essen? Nein, wir durften nicht. Step 1: find the modal in the question. Step 2: change du to ich, or ihr to wir. Step 3: say ja or nein, add the modal. Step 4: add nicht for no. Extra example: Musstest du warten? Ja, ich musste.

cards.title: School subjects and what you could do
cards.body: School subjects are short and have no article after in: in Mathe, in Kunst, in Physik. Learn in Mathe as one piece. Then say what you could or could not do: In Mathe konnte ich gut rechnen. In Kunst konnte ich nicht malen.

cards.lead: You have all the grammar for today. This card adds the school subjects, so you can talk about what you could do well and what was not allowed in each one.

deeper.text: Mathe is the everyday short form of Mathematik. Erdkunde is also called Geografie in some places. Most subject names have no plural, so you say in Physik and never in Physiken. Take one chunk, like in Biologie, and build the rest of the sentence around it.

example.en: My favourite subject was history.

cards.more: A subject is like a room with a name on the door: Mathe, Kunst, Physik. You walk in with the little word in, no article: in Mathe. Step 1: choose the room: In Kunst. Step 2: put the modal in seat 2: konnte. Step 3: add who and what: ich nicht malen. Say: In Kunst konnte ich nicht malen. Extra example: In Erdkunde konnten wir gut arbeiten. Do the same for every room.

lessons.title: Ich sollte, ich mochte: sollen and mögen, all six modals, and the sound of e
lessons.goal: Use all six modals in the past, give a reason with weil, say the e well and tell a school story in 5 sentences.

grammar.point: sollen and mögen have a one-word past too: ich sollte, ich mochte. Mögen changes g to ch. All six modals use -te, lose their dots and have the same form for ich and er/sie/es. With weil the modal goes to the very end: ..., weil ich früh aufstehen musste.
grammar.oneLine: Ich sollte leise sein. Ich mochte Mathe. Weil-clause: modal last.

mistake.why: The g of mögen becomes ch in the past: moch-. The dots disappear and -te is added, so you get mochte.

terms.meaning: a clause that starts with weil and gives a reason. The verb that changes goes to the end.
the part of a word you say louder and longer, for example the first part of Schule.
the e at the end of a word or in -te, -ten, which you say as a tiny uh.

cards.title: Before we start: all six helpers in the past
cards.body: To tell your whole school story you need the last two helpers as well: sollen and mögen. A teacher told you what to do, or you liked a subject. Today you learn Ich sollte leise sein and Ich mochte Mathe, and then all six helpers together.
steps: You already know: ich soll from A1, and from lessons 1 and 2 the past forms musste, wollte, konnte and durfte.
New today: the one-word past of sollen and mögen: ich sollte, ich mochte. Then the whole family of six, with weil and a clear way to say the e.
By the end you can: tell a school story in 5 sentences, with a reason using weil.

examples.en: I am supposed to be quiet.
examples.why: You know this: modal in part 2, infinitive at the end.

examples.de: Früher sollte ich immer leise sein.
examples.en: Earlier I was always supposed to be quiet.
examples.why: New today: sollte is the past of soll.

cards.more: Last lesson two passengers got on the time machine. Today the last two get on: sollen and mögen. Ich soll becomes ich sollte, and it means someone told me to do it. Mögen is the odd passenger: it changes a letter on the way, so ich mag becomes ich mochte. After today all six helpers can travel to the past: müssen, wollen, können, dürfen, sollen, mögen. The sentence stays the same. The helper sits in seat 2 and the second verb waits at the end.

cards.title: sollen in the past: sollte
cards.body: Sollen means to be supposed to: someone told you to do it. It has no dots, so it is as easy as wollen. Add -te: ich sollte, du solltest, wir sollten, ihr solltet. Ich sollte leise sein means I was supposed to be quiet.

examples.en: I was supposed to be quiet.
Ben was supposed to do the homework.
We were supposed to be on time.

cards.lead: You have four modals in the past. This card adds sollen, so you can say what other people told you to do, like a teacher or a parent.

deeper.text: Müssen is a duty you cannot avoid. Sollen is an order or a wish from another person, such as a teacher: Wir sollten pünktlich sein. The English is was supposed to. In this lesson sollte only talks about the past: someone told me. You do not need any other meaning of sollte yet.

example.en: Back then you were supposed to be quiet.

cards.more: Sollen is the easy one. It has no hat, so there is nothing to take off. Step 1: sollen. Step 2: take the stem: soll-. Step 3: add the past flag -te: sollte. Step 4: add the person ending if you need one: du solltest, wir sollten. Think of a teacher with a finger in the air: Ihr solltet leise sein. Somebody told you. That is sollen. Extra example: Mira sollte die Hausaufgaben machen.
steps: 1 Start with sollen.
2 Take the stem: soll-.
3 Add the past flag: sollte.
4 Add the person ending: du solltest, wir sollten.

cards.title: mögen in the past: mochte
cards.body: Mögen means to like. It is the odd one: the dots go and the g becomes ch. So ich mochte, du mochtest, wir mochten. Mögen is used with a noun: Ich mochte Mathe. Careful: möchte (would like) is not the past of mögen.

examples.en: I liked maths.
examples.why: ich mochte: g becomes ch, then -te.

examples.en: Mira liked art and music.
We did not like our teacher.

cards.lead: You know sollte now. Mögen is the last modal and it changes one letter, so this card is about the odd spelling of mochte and what mögen goes with.

deeper.text: In the present the stem is mag-: ich mag, du magst. In the past the stem is moch-. These are two different stems, so learn mochte as its own word. Möchte is a present form you already know: Ich möchte einen Kaffee. It means would like, not liked. For liked, always say mochte.

example.en: Ben liked sport.

cards.more: Mögen is the sneaky one. Three things change. The hat falls off: ö becomes o. The g turns into ch. And the past flag -te comes at the end. Step 1: mögen. Step 2: ö becomes o and g becomes ch: moch-. Step 3: add -te: mochte. Step 4: add the person ending if you need one: du mochtest, wir mochten. Say moch-te slowly. Extra example: Anna mochte Tee.
steps: 1 Start with mögen.
2 ö becomes o, g becomes ch: moch-.
3 Add the past flag: mochte.
4 Add the person ending: du mochtest, wir mochten.

cards.title: The whole family: all six modals in the past
cards.body: Now you know all six. Three rules cover them: the dots disappear, the ending -te is added, and ich and er/sie/es are the same word. One word is odd: mögen gives mochte. Say the table aloud, row by row.

examples.de: Früher musste ich lernen, aber ich wollte spielen.
examples.en: Earlier I had to study, but I wanted to play.

examples.de: Ben mochte Sport, aber er konnte nicht schwimmen.
examples.en: Ben liked sport, but he could not swim.

examples.de: Mira sollte Hausaufgaben machen, aber sie durfte nicht lange spielen.
examples.en: Mira was supposed to do homework, but she was not allowed to play for long.

cards.lead: Every modal now has a past form. This card puts all six into one table and gives you three simple rules, so you can use any of them without thinking.

deeper.text: In the table only the ich/er column and the du column are really new work. After that, wir and sie/Sie always end in -n and ihr in -t. If you know ich konnte, you also know er konnte, wir konnten and ihr konntet. Learn one column, and the rest follows. Mochte is the only spelling that needs extra care.

example.de: Wir mochten Mathe, aber wir sollten viel lernen.
example.en: We liked maths, but we were supposed to study a lot.

cards.more: Imagine six friends in a row. Each has the past flag -te on a hat. Müssen: musste. Wollen: wollte. Können: konnte. Dürfen: durfte. Sollen: sollte. Mögen: mochte. Three habits are shared: no dots, -te, and ich and er are twins. Mögen has one trick: g becomes ch. Say one row at a time: ich, du, er, wir, ihr, sie. After one round you know the whole family.

cards.title: With weil: the modal goes last
cards.body: With weil, the verb that changes goes to the end of the clause. You know this. With a modal in the past, the second verb comes first and the modal is the very last word: Ich war müde, weil ich früh aufstehen musste.

examples.de: Ich war müde, weil ich früh aufstehen musste.
examples.en: I was tired because I had to get up early.
examples.why: The modal is the last word.

examples.de: Ben war traurig, weil er nicht spielen durfte.
examples.en: Ben was sad because he was not allowed to play.
examples.why: nicht comes before the two verbs.

examples.de: Anna war froh, weil sie schon schwimmen konnte.
examples.en: Anna was happy because she could already swim.

cards.lead: You can say what you had to, could and wanted to do. This card gives the reason: you add weil, and the modal moves to the end of the little clause.

deeper.text: You can also begin with the weil clause. Then the verb of the main clause comes right after the comma, because the whole weil clause counts as one place before it: Weil ich früh aufstehen musste, war ich müde. Both orders mean the same. Use the one that sounds natural in your story.

example.de: Weil ich früh aufstehen musste, war ich müde.
example.en: Because I had to get up early, I was tired.

cards.more: A weil clause is a little train. The engine is weil. The modal is the last carriage and it always goes at the very end. Step 1: say the main sentence: Ich war müde. Step 2: add a comma and weil. Step 3: say who and what: ich früh aufstehen. Step 4: put the modal last: musste. Careful: not weil ich musste früh aufstehen. The modal is never in the middle. Extra example: Ich war froh, weil ich nicht lernen musste.

cards.title: Short past or Perfekt?
cards.body: For most verbs people use the Perfekt when they speak: Ich habe gelernt. But sein, haben and the six modals keep the short past, even in a chat: ich war, ich hatte, ich musste. Say wollte, never a Perfekt form. A Perfekt of modals exists, but it is rare.

examples.de: Gestern habe ich gelernt, weil ich eine Prüfung hatte.
examples.en: Yesterday I studied because I had an exam.
examples.why: Perfekt for lernen, short past for hatte.

examples.en: Earlier I often had hunger.

examples.de: Am Samstag habe ich Pizza gegessen.
examples.en: On Saturday I ate pizza.

cards.lead: You use the short past for six modals. This card shows when to use it and when to switch to the Perfekt, so your stories sound natural when you speak.

deeper.text: Books and the news use the short past for many more verbs, but that is a later topic. For now one safe rule is enough: war, hatte and the six modals in the short past, and every other verb in the Perfekt when you speak. You can tell a whole story with just these two tools.

example.de: Wir haben gestern gelernt, aber wir wollten spielen.
example.en: Yesterday we studied, but we wanted to play.

cards.more: Think of two tools in a toolbox. Tool 1 is the short past: for sein, haben and the six modals. Tool 2 is the Perfekt: for all the other verbs. Step 1: look at the verb. Step 2: is it sein, haben or a modal? Take tool 1. Step 3: anything else? Take tool 2. Extra example: Ich war müde und habe Tee getrunken. Both tools are in one sentence, and it sounds natural.

rows: Ich war müde. Ich hatte Hunger.
Ich musste warten. Ich konnte schwimmen.
Ich habe gelernt. Ich bin gefahren.

cards.title: Say it right: the sounds of e
cards.body: The letter e has three sounds. Long e: lesen, Tee, Schnee. Short e: Bett, essen, Fenster. And a quiet e at the end of a word or in -te, -ten: Schule, lernen, musste, wollte. The ending -er sounds like a short a: Lehrer, Schüler.

examples.en: We wanted to drink tea.
examples.why: Quiet e in wollten, long e in Tee.

examples.en: The teacher had to wait a long time.
Ben could not eat.

cards.lead: You can now build every sentence. This card is about saying the e in them well: three different sounds, and one quiet ending you will meet in every modal.

deeper.text: In German the stress is usually on the first syllable, so the endings stay weak: MUS-te, WOLL-te, KONN-te. If you say the final e loud, you sound like a beginner. Say the ending quickly and quietly. Listen to the video for this lesson and repeat every word aloud, once slowly and once at normal speed.

example.en: The pupil had to read.

cards.more: Think of the e as a singer with three voices. Voice 1 is loud and long, like in Tee. Voice 2 is short and quick, like in Bett. Voice 3 is a whisper: the e in Schule, lernen, musste. It is almost not there. Step 1: look at where the e sits. Step 2: at the end or in -te, -ten? Whisper it. Step 3: in a stressed syllable? Sing it long or short. Say musste five times with a whisper.

rows: like ay in say, held long
like a short a at the end

cards.title: Tell your school story in five sentences
cards.body: A short school story has five sentences: who you were, what you had to do, what you liked, what was not allowed, and why you felt a certain way, with weil. Use the five sentences below as a model, then change the details to tell your own story.

examples.de: Ich musste früh aufstehen und Hausaufgaben machen.
examples.en: I had to get up early and do homework.
I liked maths and art.

examples.de: Wir durften im Unterricht nicht essen.
examples.en: We were not allowed to eat in class.

cards.lead: You have every tool: six modals, weil, and the sounds. This last card puts them together in a short story, so you see how a real memory is built, one sentence at a time.

deeper.text: A story is easier when each sentence has one job. Sentence 1 sets the scene, sentences 2 to 4 give facts, and sentence 5 gives a reason. You can change any sentence. Keep the pattern: modal in part 2, second verb last, and with weil the modal at the end. Say your story aloud twice.

example.en: I was a pupil in Hamburg.

cards.more: A story is a ladder with five steps. Step 1: who I was. Step 2: what I had to do. Step 3: what I liked. Step 4: what was not allowed. Step 5: why, with weil. Climb one step at a time. Read the five model sentences aloud, then swap one detail in each: another time, another subject, another rule. In five minutes you have your own story. Short sentences are good sentences.

2 Ich musste früh aufstehen und Hausaufgaben machen.
3 Ich mochte Mathe und Kunst.
4 Wir durften im Unterricht nicht essen.
5 Ich war oft müde, weil ich früh aufstehen musste.

lessons.title: Wann Perfekt, wann kurz? War, hatte and the modals vs the Perfekt
lessons.goal: Tell what you did after school in 4 or 5 sentences, using the Perfekt for actions and war, hatte or a modal for the rest.

grammar.point: Sein, haben and the six modals use the short past (war, hatte, musste). All other verbs use the Perfekt when you talk. In one story you use both.
grammar.oneLine: Ich habe Abitur gemacht, aber ich wollte nicht studieren. Perfekt for actions, short past for war, hatte and modals.

mistake.why: Wollen is a modal, so it uses the short past: wollte in part 2, and werden stays at the end. A Perfekt with gewollt is rare and sounds heavy, and the verb order is wrong too.

terms.meaning: the spoken past: haben or sein in part 2 and a participle at the end, for example ich habe gemacht
the verb form at the end of a Perfekt sentence, for example gemacht, gegangen
the one-word past of sein, haben and the modals: war, hatte, musste

cards.title: Before we start: two ways to talk about the past
cards.body: You can already say what happened (Perfekt) and how things were (war, hatte, musste). Now you will put both into one story about your life after school. People ask this all the time: Was hast du nach der Schule gemacht? Today you learn which past to use, and when.
steps: You already know: the Perfekt with haben and sein, and the short past war, hatte and the six modals.
New today: one story that uses both, with the right past for every verb.
By the end you can: tell what you did after school, in 4 or 5 sentences, with the right past.

examples.en: I went to school.
examples.why: You know this: Perfekt, a helper verb and a participle.

examples.de: Ich habe Abitur gemacht, aber ich wollte nicht studieren.
examples.en: I did my Abitur, but I did not want to study.
examples.why: New today: Perfekt for what happened, short past for wollte, in one sentence.

cards.more: Imagine you tell a friend a story and you have two tools in your pocket. Tool one is the Perfekt: a helper and a word at the end. Tool two is a tiny short word: war, hatte, musste, wollte. Today you learn the simple rule for picking a tool. Things you did use tool one. How things were, or what you had to or wanted to do, use tool two. Then your story sounds natural, like a real German person talking.

cards.title: Two pasts, one job
cards.body: When you talk about the past, German uses two tools. Sein, haben and the six modals use one short word: war, hatte, musste. All other verbs use the Perfekt: haben or sein plus a participle at the end. Both say the same thing: it is over.

examples.de: Ich war gern in der Schule.
examples.en: I liked being at school.
I had to learn a lot.
I did my Abitur.

cards.lead: The introduction showed one story with two kinds of past. This card sorts every verb into one of two groups, so you always know which past to use.

deeper.text: Both pasts mean the same time: it is over. The difference is habit. Sein, haben and the modals are used so often that Germans keep the short word even in a chat. For all other verbs the short form sounds like a book, so people prefer the Perfekt when they talk.

example.en: Yesterday I had no time.

cards.more: Think of two boxes. In box one live only eight verbs: sein, haben, and the six modals. They have a little short word for the past: war, hatte, musste, wollte, konnte, durfte, sollte, mochte. In box two live all the other verbs: machen, gehen, lernen, and thousands more. For them you use the Perfekt, helper plus participle. Before you speak, ask: is my verb in box one? Then use the short word. If not, use the Perfekt.

rows: Ich war gern in der Schule.
müssen, wollen, können, dürfen, sollen, mögen
musste, wollte, konnte, durfte, sollte, mochte

cards.title: One story, both pasts
cards.body: In a story you switch between the two tools. Things that happen one after the other use the Perfekt. How you felt, or what you had to do, uses the short past. Gymnasium is the secondary school that leads to the Abitur.

examples.en: I went to primary school.

examples.de: Dann bin ich aufs Gymnasium gegangen.
examples.en: Then I went to the Gymnasium.

examples.de: Da war ich gern, aber ich musste viel lernen.
examples.en: I liked it there, but I had to learn a lot.

cards.lead: Card 1 gave you the two groups. Now you see them side by side in one little story about school, so you can hear how the pasts take turns in real speech.

deeper.text: A good trick: ask yourself, is this something that happened, or how things were? Things that happened (I went, I passed) are actions, so they use the Perfekt. How things were or what I had to do (I was happy, I had to learn) are states, and states use war, hatte or a modal.

example.de: Ich habe viel gelernt, und ich war müde.
example.en: I learned a lot, and I was tired.

cards.more: Picture a film. The film has scenes where something happens: you go, you pass, you start. Those scenes use the Perfekt. Between the scenes there are quiet moments where the camera shows how things were: you were happy, you had homework, you had to learn. Those moments use the short past. A good story switches between the two like a film switches between action and calm. Do not worry about being perfect. Choose by the verb and it will almost always be right.

rows: Dann bin ich aufs Gymnasium gegangen.

cards.title: War, not a Perfekt, for sein, haben and the modals
cards.body: For sein, haben and the modals you do not build a Perfekt when you talk. You use the one short word. It is shorter, and it is what Germans say. Ich war müde. Ich hatte Zeit. Ich wollte gehen. One word, no helper, no participle.

examples.en: My teacher was nice.
We had no homework.
I could already swim.

cards.lead: Card 2 mixed the two pasts. Here is the biggest shortcut of the lesson: for sein, haben and the modals you never need a helper verb in the past, only one short word.

deeper.text: In some southern regions you may hear the participle gewesen, and you can understand it. But for your own sentences, use war and hatte. They are always safe, in a chat and in an email. The modals work the same: use the short form with the other verb as an infinitive at the end.

example.de: Gestern war ich in der Schule.
example.en: Yesterday I was at school.

cards.more: Here is the shortcut. Today you say ich bin, ich habe, ich kann, ich muss, ich will. In the past you swap each of them for one little word: ich war, ich hatte, ich konnte, ich musste, ich wollte. You do not add anything. You only swap. And the rest of the sentence stays the same: the other verb is still at the end. It is the easiest part of German past. So if you are unsure, and the verb is one of these, use the short word and relax.

cards.title: The Perfekt in three steps
cards.body: All other verbs use the Perfekt. It always has the same three steps: choose the helper, make the participle, put the participle at the end. New verbs from today: abschließen, durchfallen, sitzenbleiben.

examples.en: Anna finished her training.
Ben never repeated a year.

examples.de: Leon ist in der Prüfung durchgefallen.
examples.en: Leon failed the exam.

cards.lead: Card 3 told you which verbs skip the Perfekt. This card is your checklist for all the others, including the three new verbs of this lesson: abschließen, durchfallen and sitzenbleiben.

deeper.text: Sein is used when the subject moves or something changes: gehen, kommen, durchfallen, sitzenbleiben. Learn the helper together with the participle: ist durchgefallen, ist sitzengeblieben. Verbs that start with be-, ver-, er- or end in -ieren have no ge-: besucht, studiert. Separable verbs put ge in the middle: abgeschlossen.

example.en: Mira did not fail.

cards.more: Think of building a sentence like a little train. The engine is the helper: haben or sein. It stays near the front, in seat two. The last wagon is the participle, and it goes to the very end. Between engine and wagon you can put anything: the people, the places, the times. Most verbs take haben. Verbs of moving or changing take sein. Just learn the helper together with the participle, like a pair, and the train always runs.
steps: Step 1: choose the helper: haben for most verbs, sein for going, coming and changing.
Step 2: make the participle: ge + stem + t or en. After be-, ver-, er- there is no ge. A separable verb puts ge in the middle.
Step 3: the helper is in part 2, the participle is the last word.

cards.title: Questions about the past
cards.body: You ask in the same two tools. With most verbs: Was hast du gemacht? With sein, haben and the modals: Wo warst du? Was wolltest du werden? Learn this last question as a whole chunk. It is one of the most common questions about school.

examples.de: Was hast du nach der Schule gemacht?
examples.en: What did you do after school?

examples.de: Wo warst du in den Ferien?
examples.en: Where were you in the holidays?
What did you want to become?

cards.lead: So far you built statements. Now you turn them into questions, because in a real talk about your school days somebody will always ask you: and then, what did you do?

deeper.text: A question with a question word keeps the verb in part 2: Was hast du gemacht? The helper hast sits in part 2, and the participle gemacht goes to the end, exactly like in a statement. Questions without a question word start with the verb: Hast du Abitur gemacht? Warst du gern in der Schule?

example.en: Did you pass the exam?

cards.more: A question is a sentence with the two parts swapped. If you say Du hast Abitur gemacht, you can turn it into a question with a question word at the front: Wann hast du Abitur gemacht? The helper still sits in seat two, and the participle still waits at the end. Without a question word, the helper jumps to seat one: Hast du Abitur gemacht? The short past works the same way: Wo warst du? Warst du gern in der Schule?

rows: Was hast du nach der Schule gemacht?
Wo warst du in den Ferien?
Wann hast du das Abitur gemacht?

cards.title: Your life in five stations
cards.body: Tell a life like a timeline, station by station. Each station gets the right past. Time words help the listener: mit sechs Jahren, dann, danach, vor drei Jahren. The time word can stand first, and the verb still comes second.

examples.de: Mit sechs Jahren bin ich in die Schule gekommen.
examples.en: At six I started school.

examples.de: Dann habe ich das Abitur gemacht.
examples.en: Then I did my Abitur.

examples.de: Vor drei Jahren habe ich die Ausbildung abgeschlossen.
examples.en: Three years ago I finished my training.

cards.lead: You know both tools and the question forms. This card puts them on a timeline of five stations, from the first school day to the first job, with the right past at each stop.

deeper.text: Vor + dative looks back: vor drei Jahren means three years ago. You know seit with the present: seit drei Jahren wohne ich hier. Vor goes with the past tense. Both are time phrases, so they can stand in position 1, and the verb stays in part 2.

example.de: Vor zwei Jahren habe ich in Berlin gewohnt.
example.en: Two years ago I lived in Berlin.

cards.more: Imagine a path with five stones. Stone one: first day at school. Stone two: the school years. Stone three: the Abitur. Stone four: training. Stone five: your first job. You walk along the path and say one sentence at each stone. Culture note: in Germany many young people do an Ausbildung, which is training in a company and a school together, after the Abitur or instead of it. Some also go on a Schüleraustausch, a school exchange, to another country.
steps: Station 1, Grundschule: Ich bin mit sechs Jahren in die Schule gekommen.
Station 2, school years: Ich musste viel lernen. Ich hatte immer Hausaufgaben.
Station 3, Abitur: Ich habe das Abitur gemacht.
Station 4, Ausbildung: Vor drei Jahren habe ich die Ausbildung abgeschlossen.
Station 5, first job: Danach hatte ich einen Job im Restaurant.

cards.title: Two pasts with weil
cards.body: Give a reason with weil. The verb goes to the end, as in chapter 1. With the short past this is easy: war, hatte or musste is the last word. A modal also has its infinitive in front of it: weil ich lernen musste.

examples.de: Ich bin nicht gekommen, weil ich krank war.
examples.en: I did not come because I was ill.

examples.de: Ich habe viel gelernt, weil ich eine Prüfung hatte.
examples.en: I learned a lot because I had an exam.

examples.de: Ich bin zu Hause geblieben, weil ich lernen musste.
examples.en: I stayed at home because I had to learn.

cards.lead: On card 6 you told a life in order. Now you add the reason with weil and a short past verb, a natural next step once you say what happened.

deeper.text: Only the verb with the personal ending moves to the end. In the main part, hat or ist stays in part 2 and the participle is last. In the weil part there is usually just one verb, so war, hatte or musste is the very last word. With a modal, the infinitive stands before it.

example.de: Ich war müde, weil ich lernen musste.
example.en: I was tired because I had to learn.

cards.more: Weil is a little magnet. It pulls the changing verb to the very end of its part. In the main part the sentence stays normal: helper in seat two, participle at the end. After the comma, weil starts a new part, and that part ends with the verb: weil ich krank war, weil ich eine Prüfung hatte, weil ich lernen musste. Think of weil as a full stop for the verb. The little word ends the sentence.

lessons.title: Mit meinem Lehrer, bei meiner Klasse: all possessives in the dative
lessons.goal: Say who you do things with at school, using any possessive article in the dative after mit, bei, von, zu, aus and nach.

grammar.point: After mit, bei, von, zu, aus and nach the possessive takes dative endings: -em (der, das), -er (die), -en (plural, and the noun gets -n). This works for mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer and Ihr. The noun decides the ending, not the owner.
grammar.oneLine: Ich spreche mit meinem Lehrer. Mit meiner Freundin. Mit meinen Freunden. Ending -em, -er, -en.

mistake.why: Mit is always followed by the dative. Freundin is feminine, so the dative of meine is meiner: -er like der in der Freundin.

terms.meaning: a word that shows who owns something: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr
the case after mit, bei, von, zu, aus and nach, and for the receiver of something
the letters at the end of the possessive: -em, -er, -en

cards.title: Before we start: with my teacher, with our class
cards.body: At school you do everything with someone: with your teacher, with your classmates, with your friends. To say who, you need a possessive article after mit, bei, von and zu. You know mein in the dative. Today you learn all of them: dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr.
steps: You already know: mit meinem Chef, mit meinen Kindern, and Das ist unser Lehrer.
New today: the dative endings for every possessive: mit unserem Lehrer, mit eurer Klasse, mit ihren Mitschülern.
By the end you can: say who you do things with, with any possessive, in 4 or 5 sentences.

examples.en: I speak with my boss.
examples.why: You know this: mein in the dative after mit.

examples.en: I speak with our teacher.
examples.why: New today: unser follows the same pattern, with the ending -em.

cards.more: Imagine a little word that goes before the person: mit, bei, von, zu. It says "with", "at", "from", "to". After it, the word for my, your, his or our wears a little coat. You already know the coat for mein: meinem, meiner, meinen. Today you learn that every other possessive wears the same coat. So you learn one coat, and it fits seven words. That is the whole lesson. Then you can say who you do things with at school.

cards.title: Mein in the dative: a quick recap
cards.body: You know mein in the dative from A1. The endings copy der, die, das, die: dem, der, dem, den. So der and das words end in -em, die words end in -er, and the plural ends in -en. Learn the clue: -m, -r, -m, -n.

examples.en: I speak with my teacher.

examples.de: Ich gehe mit meiner Freundin zur Schule.
examples.en: I go to school with my friend.
I play with my friends.

cards.lead: The introduction showed that mein is only the first of seven. Before we add the others, this card refreshes the four endings you already know, so you have a pattern to copy.

deeper.text: Mein has no ending in the nominative for der and das words (mein Lehrer, mein Kind), but it gets one in the dative: meinem. The clue is the article: dem, der, dem, den. If you know that mit takes the dative, and you know the article, you know the ending.

example.de: Ich wohne mit meinem Kind zusammen.
example.en: I live together with my child.

cards.more: Here is a little trick. Whatever the article is in the dative, the possessive copies it. Der Lehrer becomes dem Lehrer, so mein Lehrer becomes meinem Lehrer. Die Freundin becomes der Freundin, so meiner Freundin. And the plural? Den, so meinen, and the noun gets an n. Culture note: in German schools you say Frau or Herr and the surname, for example Frau Weber. From the Gymnasium on, students usually say Sie to teachers.

cards.title: All possessives, one pattern
cards.body: Dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer and Ihr take exactly the same endings: -em, -er, -em, -en. Careful with euer: it loses an e. You say eurem, eurer, euren. Unser can keep both e: unserem, unserer, unseren.

examples.en: I speak with our teacher.
We play with your (plural) class.
I play with your friends.

cards.lead: Card 1 showed the endings for mein. This card shows that dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer and Ihr copy them exactly, so one table covers all seven.

deeper.text: Ihr (her, their) and Ihr with a capital I (your, formal) look the same and take the same endings: mit Ihrem Lehrer, mit Ihrer Klasse. Euer is the only one that drops its e before an ending. All the others just add the ending to the basic form.

example.en: I speak with your teacher (formal).

cards.more: Picture seven little words in a row: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr. In the dative they all wear the same coat: -em for der and das words, -er for die words, -en for the plural. The only little surprise is euer. It drops its middle e and wears the coat on top: eurem, eurer, euren. If you know the coat, you can say mit any of them. You do not learn seven tables. You learn one.

cards.title: Prepositions that always take the dative
cards.body: Six small words always want the dative: mit, bei, von, zu, aus, nach. With a possessive, zu does not become zum: you say zu meinem Lehrer, zu meiner Klasse. The contraction zum and zur only works with the plain articles.

examples.de: Ich gehe mit meinem Mitschüler nach Hause.
examples.en: I go home with my classmate.
I live with my aunt.
I go to my teacher.

cards.lead: You have the endings. Now you need to know when to use them. This card lists the six prepositions that always trigger the dative, with a possessive after each.

deeper.text: Learn the six as a little song: mit, bei, von, zu, aus, nach. After any of them, the next group of words is dative. A possessive in that group wears -em, -er or -en. Nach with a time word is also dative: nach meiner Schulzeit means after my school days.

example.de: Ich habe nach meiner Schulzeit eine Lehre gemacht.
example.en: After my school days I did an apprenticeship.

cards.more: Six little words open the dative door: mit, bei, von, zu, aus, nach. When you say one of them, the next group of words wears the dative coat. That is the only rule. With a possessive it is the same: bei meiner Tante, von seinem Lehrer, zu unserer Klasse. Do not say zum or zur here. Zum and zur are only little short forms for zu dem and zu der. With mein, dein and the others you say the whole word zu.

rows: Das ist ein Freund von seinem Bruder.
Nach meiner Schulzeit habe ich studiert.

cards.title: The plural: -en and one extra n
cards.body: In the dative plural two things change: the possessive ends in -en, and the noun gets an extra -n. Mit meinen Mitschülern. But if the plural noun already ends in -n or -s, nothing is added: mit meinen Lehrerinnen, mit meinen Autos.

examples.en: I learn with my classmates.
We play with our friends.
I speak with my teachers (female).

cards.lead: So far the examples used a single person. Now you talk about several people. Here the possessive and the noun both change, and this card shows the plural -n rule step by step.

deeper.text: You know this rule from A1: in the dative plural the noun ends in -n. Mit Kindern, mit Freunden. The rule is not new, but now the possessive shows it too: meinen. Words that already end in -n or -s (Lehrerinnen, Autos) stay as they are, because there is no room for another n.

example.en: I drive with my children.

cards.more: Two little jobs in the plural: first the possessive gets -en, then the noun gets an n. Think of it as two letters, e and n, on the possessive, and one extra n on the noun. Freund becomes Freunde in the plural, and Freunden after mit. Mitschüler stays the same in the plural, but gets an n: mit meinen Mitschülern. The mistake to avoid is mit meinen Mitschüler. Always add the n. Lehrerinnen and Autos are the two easy words: they stay as they are.

cards.title: Sein or ihr? The noun decides the ending
cards.body: Sein means his, ihr means her or their. That choice depends on the owner. But the ending depends on the noun that follows. Ben spricht mit seinem Bruder. Mira spricht mit ihrem Bruder. Both brothers are masculine, so both end in -em.

examples.en: Ben speaks with his brother.
Mira speaks with her brother.
Mira plays with her sister.

cards.lead: Cards 3 and 4 showed the six prepositions and the plural. Now a common worry: how do you choose between sein and ihr, and where does the ending come from?

deeper.text: Do two steps in this order: first choose the word, sein for he or it, ihr for she or they. Then choose the ending by looking at the noun, not at the owner. A woman with a brother says ihrem Bruder, because Bruder is masculine. A man with a sister says seiner Schwester, because Schwester is feminine.

example.en: Ben lives with his aunt.

cards.more: There are two little questions. Question one: whose is it? A man, so sein. A woman, so ihr. Question two: what is the noun? Brother, masculine, so -em. Sister, feminine, so -er. You never mix the two questions. The owner chooses the word. The noun chooses the ending. So Mira, a woman, with her brother is ihrem Bruder, and Ben, a man, with his sister is seiner Schwester. Say it slowly, and the pattern is clear.

cards.title: Wem? Ask and answer
cards.body: Wem asks for a person in the dative. After a preposition, put the preposition in front: mit wem, bei wem, von wem, zu wem. The short answer is only the preposition and the group of words: Mit meinem Bruder. Bei meiner Tante.

examples.de: Mit wem gehst du zur Schule?
examples.en: With whom do you go to school?
With whom do you live?

examples.de: Von wem hast du das Buch?
examples.en: Who did you get the book from?

cards.lead: You can now answer with a possessive. This card gives you the question, so you can also ask: with whom, at whose place, from whom, to whom.

deeper.text: Wem is the dative of wer. You know it from A1: Wem gehört das? After a preposition you put the preposition first. In German the question starts with the preposition, not with the word wem alone. The answer can be short, because the question already contains the verb: Mit meinem Bruder.

example.en: Whom are you going to?

cards.more: A question about a person has two pieces: the little preposition and wem. Put them together at the front: mit wem, bei wem, von wem, zu wem. Then the verb, then du. The answer only needs the two pieces too: the preposition and the possessive group. Mit meinem Bruder. Bei meiner Tante. Von meinem Lehrer. Zu meiner Freundin. You do not have to say a whole sentence. A short answer is perfectly normal in German.

cards.title: Three steps to the right ending
cards.body: When you are unsure, go through three steps. First find the preposition. Then find the gender of the noun. Then choose the ending. This works for every possessive, and for every sentence in this lesson.

examples.en: I play with my friend.
I play with my friend (female).

cards.lead: You have all the pieces: the endings, the prepositions, the plural and the owner. This card puts them into a routine of three steps that you can use every time you are unsure.

deeper.text: The dative with a preposition has a twin: the accusative. Without a preposition from our list, a direct object is accusative: Ich sehe meinen Lehrer. After mit it is dative: Ich spreche mit meinem Lehrer. The only thing that changes is the ending of mein: -en or -em. The preposition decides.

example.de: Ich sehe meinen Lehrer, aber ich spreche mit meinem Lehrer.
example.en: I see my teacher, but I speak with my teacher.

cards.more: Imagine a little checklist you read before you speak. One: which small word is in front? Mit, bei, von, zu, aus, nach? Then you know it is dative. Two: is the noun der, die, das or plural? Three: put the coat on. Der or das gets -em, die gets -er, plural gets -en. And a small contrast to remember: without mit, a direct object is accusative: Ich sehe meinen Lehrer. With mit it is dative: mit meinem Lehrer. So the little word in front decides.
steps: Step 1: find the preposition. Mit, bei, von, zu, aus or nach means dative.
Step 2: find the noun and its gender: der or das, die, or plural.
Step 3: choose the ending: -em for der and das, -er for die, -en for the plural (and the noun gets -n).

lessons.title: Ich zeige meiner Lehrerin mein Heft: the dative as the person
lessons.goal: Say who gets something and who something belongs to, using a possessive in the dative for the person and the accusative for the thing.

grammar.point: With geben, zeigen, leihen and verraten the person is in the dative and comes first, the thing is in the accusative. Helfen, gehören, antworten and gefallen have only a dative person. The possessive ending shows the role: meinem Bruder (dative), meinen Bruder (accusative).
grammar.oneLine: Ich zeige meiner Lehrerin mein Heft. Dative person first, accusative thing second.

mistake.wrong: Ich zeige mein Lehrer mein Heft.
mistake.right: Ich zeige meinem Lehrer mein Heft.
mistake.why: The person who gets something is in the dative. Lehrer is masculine, so the dative of mein is meinem. Only the thing, mein Heft, stays in the accusative.

terms.meaning: the person who gets something or to whom something belongs: meinem Bruder
the thing that is given or shown: mein Heft
the question word for the dative person: Wem gehört das Lineal?

cards.title: Before we start: who gets it?
cards.body: At school things move from person to person: you lend a ruler, you show a notebook, you help a friend. To say who gets something, or who something belongs to, you use the dative. You know mir and dir. Today the person is a noun with a possessive: meinem Bruder, meiner Lehrerin.
steps: You already know: Das gehört mir. Die Jacke gefällt mir. Ich helfe dir.
New today: the dative person with a possessive and a noun, and a second thing in the accusative: Ich leihe meiner Freundin mein Lineal.
By the end you can: say who gets what, and who something belongs to, in 4 or 5 sentences.

examples.en: I like the jacket.
examples.why: You know this: a small word like mir after the verb.

examples.en: The notebook belongs to my brother.
examples.why: New today: mir becomes meinem Bruder, a possessive with a noun.

cards.more: Imagine you hold a ruler in your hand and give it to someone. The someone is the dative person: you say wem, to whom. You already know the small words for the person: mir, dir, ihm, ihr. Today the person gets a longer name, like my brother or my teacher. The small word is replaced by the group with mein and a noun. The ruler, the thing you give, is a second group. So you learn who gets it and what it is.

cards.title: Wem? Verbs that only want the dative
cards.body: Wem asks for the person who gets or owns something. Four verbs have only a dative person and no thing: helfen, gehören, antworten, gefallen. With a possessive: Ich helfe meinem Bruder. Das Lineal gehört meiner Schwester.

examples.en: Whose ruler is that?
I help my brother.
I answer my teacher.

cards.lead: The introduction showed mir and meinem Bruder side by side. This card lists the four verbs that need only a dative person, so you know where the dative comes from.

deeper.text: These four verbs always take the dative, never the accusative. You know helfen, gehören and gefallen from A1 with mir and dir. Antworten works the same: you answer someone. The person goes in the dative, and with a possessive it wears -em, -er or -en.

example.en: My mother likes the book.

cards.more: Think of four verbs that have a little hook for a person. Helfen: you help someone. Gehören: something belongs to someone. Antworten: you answer someone. Gefallen: something pleases someone. Ask wem? to find the person. The person gets the dative coat: meinem Bruder, meiner Lehrerin. The thing, if there is one, is the subject: Das Lineal gehört meiner Schwester. The ruler belongs. The sister is the one it belongs to.

cards.title: Two objects: the person and the thing
cards.body: Verbs like geben and zeigen have two objects: the person who gets something (dative) and the thing (accusative). Ich zeige meiner Lehrerin mein Heft. Ask wem? for the person and was? for the thing.

cards.lead: Card 1 had only a person. Now there are two groups after the verb: the person who gets something and the thing itself. This card shows how to tell them apart.

deeper.text: The thing is the accusative object and the person is the dative object. Ask wem? and you find the person. Ask was? and you find the thing. With a feminine or plural thing, the possessive shows the accusative: meine Tasche, meine Hefte. With a neuter thing, mein has no ending: mein Heft.

example.de: Mira schenkt ihrer Mutter ein Buch.
example.en: Mira gives her mother a book.

cards.more: Imagine a little gift. The giver says: I give. Who gets the gift? My teacher: meiner Lehrerin. What is the gift? My notebook: mein Heft. So you build the sentence with the person first and the gift second. You can check with two questions: Wem zeige ich etwas? Meiner Lehrerin. Was zeige ich? Mein Heft. The person wears the dative coat. The gift wears the accusative coat. Two groups, two coats.

cards.title: Order and endings: dative first
cards.body: When both are nouns, the dative person comes first, then the thing. The ending changes with the role: the same word is meinem Bruder as the dative person and meinen Bruder as the accusative. The role decides the ending, not the noun alone.

examples.en: I see my brother.
I help my brother.

examples.de: Ich zeige meinem Bruder meinen Taschenrechner.
examples.en: I show my brother my calculator.

cards.lead: Cards 1 and 2 gave you the roles. Now you compare them side by side, and you learn which one comes first. The same word can have two different endings.

deeper.text: The ending of a possessive tells you its role. For a masculine noun the accusative ends in -en and the dative in -em: meinen Bruder, meinem Bruder. For a feminine noun the dative has -er and the accusative has -e: meiner Schwester, meine Schwester. For a neuter noun the accusative has no ending: mein Kind.

example.de: Ich zeige meiner Schwester meine Tasche.
example.en: I show my sister my bag.

cards.more: Look at the little word before the noun. Does it end in -em, -er or -en with the noun Bruder, Lehrerin, Kind? Then it is dative, the person who gets something. Does it end in -en, -e or nothing? Then it is accusative, the thing. Meinem Bruder: dative. Meinen Bruder: accusative. A good habit is to say the dative first, the person, and then the thing: Ich zeige meinem Bruder meinen Taschenrechner. Person first, thing second. And one more caution: the verbs helfen, gehören, antworten, gefallen only ever have the dative.

cards.title: Lend, borrow, tell
cards.body: Three useful school verbs: leihen (to lend), borgen (to borrow) and verraten (to tell, to give away). Leihen takes two objects: Ich leihe meinem Freund meinen Taschenrechner. For borgen you say von and the dative: Ich borge von meiner Freundin ein Lineal.

cards.lead: You have the pattern. This card applies it to three verbs that school life needs every day, and it shows the participles you need for the Perfekt.

deeper.text: Von is a dative preposition from lesson 5: von meiner Freundin. So with borgen the person stands behind von, and the thing is the accusative. Leihen and verraten take the dative person directly. Verraten starts with ver-, so its participle has no ge-: verraten. The participle of leihen is irregular: geliehen.

example.de: Anna hat von ihrem Bruder einen Taschenrechner geborgt.
example.en: Anna borrowed a calculator from her brother.

cards.more: Three small verbs. Leihen is to lend: you give something for a while. Borgen is to borrow: you take something for a while, and you say von for the person. Verraten is to tell a secret, or to give something away. Leihen and verraten are like geben: person first, thing second. Borgen is the little exception: it needs von. For the Perfekt: zeigen is gezeigt, leihen is geliehen, borgen is geborgt, and verraten stays verraten, because of the ver-.

cards.title: Short answers with wem
cards.body: The question Wem gibst du das Heft? has a short answer: just the dative group. Meinem Bruder. Meiner Mutter. You can also answer in a full sentence. Short answers are very natural in German, especially when you talk.

cards.lead: You can now ask and answer with the dative. This card shows the shortest possible answer, a bare dative group, because in real talk nobody repeats the whole sentence.

deeper.text: A short answer repeats only the new information, and the new information is the person. So it stands in the dative: Meinem Bruder. If the thing is a pronoun or a name, the order changes, but that comes later. For now: noun person first, noun thing second, and no pronoun for the thing.

example.en: Who do you help?

cards.more: When somebody asks wem, they ask for one person. So you do not need a whole sentence. You only need the group with the dative coat: meinem Bruder, meiner Mutter, meinen Eltern, unserem Lehrer. The question already says what happens. Your short answer only fills the blank. It is like answering Where? with Berlin. Short and clear. If you want to be polite and full, you can also say the whole sentence: Ich gebe das Heft meiner Mutter.

Ich leihe meiner Freundin mein Lineal.

cards.title: The past with a person
cards.body: Both pasts from this chapter work with a dative person. With a modal, the modal is part 2 and the infinitive is last: Wir mussten unserer Lehrerin die Hausaufgaben zeigen. With the Perfekt, the participle is last: Ich habe meinem Bruder mein Heft gezeigt.

examples.en: My teacher wanted to help my class.

examples.de: Wir mussten unserer Lehrerin die Hausaufgaben zeigen.

examples.en: I showed my brother my notebook.

cards.lead: You know the pasts from lesson 4 and the dative person from this lesson. Here they work together in one sentence, with the verbs at the end where they belong.

deeper.text: Nothing changes inside the group of person and thing. The only question is where the verbs go. A modal in the short past stays in part 2, and the infinitive moves to the end. In the Perfekt, haben stays in part 2 and the participle moves to the end. In both, person and thing stay in the middle.

example.de: Ich konnte meinem Freund mein Lineal leihen.
example.en: I could lend my friend my ruler.

cards.more: Imagine the verbs are two bookends. One bookend stands in seat two. The other stands at the very end. Everything else, the person and the thing, sits in between. With a modal, the bookends are the modal and the infinitive. With the Perfekt, they are haben and the participle. The dative person comes first, then the thing. So you can say: Mein Lehrer wollte meiner Klasse helfen. Or: Ich habe meinem Bruder mein Heft gezeigt. The middle never changes.

cards.title: Three steps: who gets it?
cards.body: When you are unsure, ask three questions. Who gets it? That is the dative person. What is it? That is the accusative thing. Then say it: person first, then the thing. In Germany, the Ranzen is the school bag of a primary school child. Later you carry a Schultasche.

examples.en: I lend my friend my ruler.

cards.lead: You now have all the pieces: the verbs, the roles, the order and the pasts. This card gives you a three-step routine that you can use whenever a sentence has a person and a thing.

deeper.text: Always check the gender of the person first. Lehrerin is feminine: meiner. Lehrer is masculine: meinem. Then check the thing: Heft is neuter, so mein stays without an ending. Taschenrechner is masculine, so meinen. The two groups have different endings because they have different jobs.

example.de: Ich borge von meinem Lehrer ein Wörterbuch.
example.en: I borrow a dictionary from my teacher.

cards.more: Here is the routine. First question: who gets it? Find the person, like my teacher, and put the dative coat on: meinem Lehrer or meiner Lehrerin. Second question: what is it? Find the thing, like my notebook, and put the accusative coat on: mein Heft or meinen Taschenrechner. Third: say it, person first. Ich zeige meiner Lehrerin mein Heft. One last note: the school bag a small child carries in Germany is called Ranzen. Later it is a Schultasche.

Step 2: what is it? Find the thing and use the accusative: mein Heft, meinen Taschenrechner, meine Tasche.
Step 3: say it, with the person first: Ich zeige meiner Lehrerin mein Heft.
