lessons.title: der, ein, mein, dieser: all the articles in three cases
lessons.goal: Choose the right article form (nominative, accusative, dative) in school sentences, and say where you are and where you go.

grammar.point: Articles change with the case. Nominative: der, die, das. Accusative: only the masculine changes (den, einen, diesen). Dative: dem, der, dem, den + n (einem, einer, einem, keinen + n). Three questions find the case: wer or was? wen or was? wem? After in, auf and an: wo? takes the dative, wohin? takes the accusative.
grammar.oneLine: Ich bin in der Aula. Ich gehe in die Aula. Wo? dative, wohin? accusative.

mistake.why: Gehen is a movement, so you ask wohin? and use the accusative: die Aula. In der Aula only says where you stay.

terms.meaning: the form for who or what does something: der Lehrer ist nett
the form for what or whom you see, have or need: ich sehe den Lehrer
the form for to or with whom, and after mit: ich helfe dem Lehrer
the job of a noun in the sentence: nominative, accusative or dative

cards.title: Before we start: one grid for all articles
cards.body: At school you say: Der Lehrer ist nett. Ich sehe den Lehrer. Ich spreche mit dem Lehrer. It is one teacher, but the article changes three times. Today you put every article into one grid, so you can pick the right one fast and with confidence.
steps: You already know: den and einen (A1 chapter 4), dem and einem after mit (A1 chapter 7), and meinem and meiner earlier in this chapter.
New today: one grid with der, den and dem side by side, and three questions that tell you which form to pick.
By the end you can: choose the right article in six school sentences.

examples.en: I see the teacher.
examples.why: You know this: den after sehen.

examples.en: I talk to the teacher.
examples.why: You know this: dem after mit.

examples.en: I go into the hall.
examples.why: New today: why die here, but in der Aula when you stay?

cards.more: Think of a wardrobe with three drawers. Every noun has the same three drawers: one for who does it, one for what you see, one for to whom. The article is the label on the drawer. Der Lehrer, den Lehrer, dem Lehrer: same teacher, three labels. Today you see all drawers in one picture, and you learn three little questions that tell you which drawer to open. After that, choosing an article is no longer guessing.

cards.title: The grid for der, die, das
cards.body: Der, die, das change with the job of the noun in the sentence. Only the masculine form changes between who does it and what you see: der becomes den. In the dative the forms are dem, der, dem, and den + n for the plural.

examples.en: The teacher is nice.
I see the teacher.
Frau Weber helps the class.
examples.why: Dative: die becomes der for feminine.

cards.lead: In the introduction you saw der, den and dem for one teacher. On this card: the full grid for der, die, das and plural, so you can see every form in one place.

deeper.text: Only the masculine form changes between the nominative and the accusative: der becomes den. Feminine, neuter and plural look the same in both. So the real choice is often between "the same" and the dative. In the plural dative the noun also gets an -n, if it does not already end in -n: den Lehrern, den Klassen.

example.en: I know the class.

cards.more: Look at the grid like a street map with three streets: nominative, accusative, dative. Walk down each street and read the four stops: der, die, das, die. On the first street you are at home: der, die, das, die. On the second street only one house is different: den. On the third street everything is new: dem, der, dem, den. Learn the third street well. It is the longest one.

cards.title: The grid for ein, kein, mein
cards.body: Ein, kein and mein follow one pattern. In the nominative, masculine and neuter have no ending: ein Lehrer, mein Heft. The accusative masculine gets -en: einen. The dative gets -em, -er, -em and -en + n. For the plural, kein and mein add the endings of the plural: keine, meine.

examples.en: That is my exercise book.
I do not have a timetable.
I talk to a teacher.

cards.lead: You just saw the grid for der, die, das. On this card: the same grid for ein, kein and mein, so you can say a, no and my in every job.

deeper.text: Ein-words are easy to remember: they have no ending exactly where der-words have a different word, in the masculine and neuter nominative. Ein Lehrer, ein Heft, but der Lehrer, das Heft. Everywhere else ein-words copy the der-word endings: -en, -e, -em, -er. Say it aloud: ein, einen, einem.

example.en: We have no homework.

cards.more: Imagine ein-words as der-words with their last letters cut off in two spots. Der Lehrer becomes ein Lehrer, das Heft becomes ein Heft. In all other spots they wear the same ending as der-words. Step 1: pick the case. Step 2: pick the gender. Step 3: add the ending: nothing, -en, -e, -em, -er. Kein and mein are twins of ein and use the very same endings. Only the plural is special: keine, meine.
steps: 1 Pick the case.
2 Pick the gender.
3 Add the ending: nothing, -en, -e, -em, -er.

cards.title: dieser, diese, dieses and welcher
cards.body: Dieser (this) and welcher (which) use the same endings as der-words. Masculine: dieser, diesen, diesem. Feminine: diese, diese, dieser. Neuter: dieses, dieses, diesem. Plural: diese, diese, diesen + n. Welcher works the same way: welche Schule, welchen Lehrer.

examples.en: This school is big.
I know this teacher.
I study with this exercise book.

cards.lead: You know ein-words now. On this card: dieser and welcher, which borrow their endings from der, die, das, so you can point at things and ask which one.

deeper.text: Dieser and welcher are called der-words, because they end like der: -er, -en, -em, -e. If you know the der-grid, you know these two as well. A question with welcher always matches the noun: Welche Schule? Welchen Lehrer? Mit welchem Heft? Take the answer from the question and keep the ending.

example.en: Which teacher do you know?

cards.more: Dieser is like a pointing finger: this one. Welcher is a question mark: which one? Both copy the ending from der, die, das. Der Lehrer: dieser Lehrer. Den Lehrer: diesen Lehrer. Dem Lehrer: diesem Lehrer. The ending is the same, only the first letters change. If you forget, write the der-form next to it, read the ending, and copy it. That is a safe little trick for every sentence.

cards.title: Which case? Ask three questions
cards.body: To find the case, ask a question. Wer or was does it? Nominative. Wen or was? Accusative. Wem? Dative. The verb often decides: sein and bleiben take the nominative, haben, sehen, brauchen and lesen the accusative, helfen, gehören, gefallen and antworten the dative. Prepositions like mit also take the dative.

examples.en: Who helps the teacher?
examples.why: Wem? gives the dative: dem Lehrer.

examples.en: Ben needs a timetable.
The exercise book belongs to the teacher.

cards.lead: You have the grid. On this card: the three questions that tell you which row to use, plus ten verbs that always choose the same case.

deeper.text: Learn the verbs together with their case. Helfen, gehören, gefallen and antworten take the dative even though they feel like a normal verb. You cannot guess it, you must know it. Write each of them with a tiny example: Ich helfe dem Lehrer. Das Heft gehört dem Lehrer. A small example in your head saves you every time.

example.en: The teacher likes the school.

cards.more: Three questions are three keys. Wer or was? That key opens the nominative door. Wen or was? That key opens the accusative door. Wem? That key opens the dative door. Put the verb in front of the key: Wer ist? Wen sehe ich? Wem helfe ich? The answer to the question is your noun, and its article takes the form of the door. Ten verbs are your cheat sheet, you learn them once.

cards.title: wo? or wohin? in school places
cards.body: With in, auf and an, the question decides. Wo? is where you stay: dative. Wohin? is where you go: accusative. In der Aula, but in die Aula. Im and ins are short forms: in dem becomes im, in das becomes ins. Movement words like gehen and fahren ask wohin?

examples.en: We are in the hall.
We go into the hall.
Ben plays on the sports field.

cards.lead: You know the three questions. On this card: wo? and wohin? with school places, so you can say where you are and where you are going.

deeper.text: Only the feminine and masculine places show the difference clearly: der Aula against die Aula, dem Sportplatz against den Sportplatz. Neuter places use short forms: im Schulgebäude, but ins Schulgebäude. Look at the verb. Sein, bleiben, warten and spielen describe a place where you stay. Gehen, fahren and laufen describe a way.

example.en: Mira goes to the computer room.

cards.more: Picture a door. If you stand inside, you ask wo? and you say in der Aula, in the dative. If you walk through the door, you ask wohin? and you say in die Aula, in the accusative. Step 1: look at the verb. Step 2: stay or move? Step 3: pick dative for stay, accusative for move. Step 4: read the grid. The two sentences look almost the same, but the meaning is different.

cards.title: Spot and fix the mistake
cards.body: Learners often pick the right row but the wrong form. Read each sentence and ask three things: which noun, which question, which form? Then fix it. The mistakes below are the most common ones. Read the wrong sentence aloud and listen: it often sounds odd.

examples.en: I go into the hall.
Ben helps the teacher.
I do not have a timetable.

cards.lead: Now you can pick every form. On this card: six wrong sentences and their fixes, so you learn to spot a mistake before you say it.

deeper.text: A mistake is useful: it shows exactly which question you skipped. If you see in der with a verb of movement, the question wohin? was skipped. If you see der Lehrer after sehen, the accusative was skipped. Say the wrong sentence once, then say the right one three times. The right one then sticks in your ear.

example.en: We wait on the sports field.

cards.more: Be a detective. You get a sentence. Step 1: find the noun and its article. Step 2: find the verb. Step 3: ask the question: wer, wen, wem, wo or wohin? Step 4: compare the article with the grid. If it does not match, you found the culprit. Then fix only that one word and read the sentence again. Detectives always check twice.

cards.title: Three steps for every article
cards.body: You can pick the right article in three steps. First find the gender of the noun: der, die, das or plural. Second find the case with the question. Third pick the form from the grid. Do this slowly three or four times and it becomes quick, like a reflex.

examples.en: I go by school bus.
examples.why: Gender: der. Question: mit, so dative: dem.

examples.en: Mira goes into the swimming hall.
examples.why: Gender: die. Question: wohin? so accusative: die.

examples.en: Leon waits on the school yard.
examples.why: Gender: der. Question: wo? so dative: dem.

cards.lead: You can spot mistakes now. This is the last step: three steps that put the whole grid to work, so you can choose an article in any sentence.

deeper.text: The steps always run in the same order: gender, question, form. Skipping the question is the biggest risk. A small habit helps: before you say a noun with an article, whisper the question in your head. It takes one second. After a week you will not whisper any more, because you simply know.

example.en: Anna helps a teacher.

cards.more: A recipe has three steps and you do them in order. Step 1: gender. Is it der, die, das or plural? Step 2: question. Wer, wen, wem, wo or wohin? Step 3: pick the form. Ask yourself the question, find the row in the grid, find the column of the gender, and read the word. Done. Two solved examples above show the whole recipe in action: read them again slowly.
steps: 1 Find the gender: der, die, das or plural.
2 Ask the question: wer, wen, wem, wo or wohin?
3 Pick the form from the grid.

lessons.title: Meiner Meinung nach: give your opinion and use set phrases
lessons.goal: Give an opinion with a reason, ask for opinions, and agree or disagree, using set phrases (Redemittel).

grammar.point: Opinion phrases: Ich finde + thing + adjective; Ich denke, + normal sentence; Meiner Meinung nach + verb in position 2. Ich bin dafür / dagegen; für / gegen + accusative. Zustimmen and widersprechen take the dative: Ich stimme dir zu, Ich widerspreche dir. Reasons with weil: the verb goes to the end.
grammar.oneLine: Meiner Meinung nach ist das gut. The verb comes right after the phrase.

mistake.wrong: Meiner Meinung nach das ist gut.
mistake.right: Meiner Meinung nach ist das gut.
mistake.why: Meiner Meinung nach fills position 1, so the verb ist must be position 2. Then comes the subject das.

terms.meaning: ready-made phrases for a purpose, such as giving an opinion or agreeing
what you think about something
the form for to or with whom: dir, mir, ihm, dem Lehrer
a verb that splits: ich stimme dir zu

cards.title: Before we start: say what you think
cards.body: Wie findest du Schuluniformen? In a talk, in an exam and in a chat, people ask for your opinion all the time. Today you learn ready-made set phrases for it. You do not build every sentence from zero: you take a ready piece and add your idea and your reason.
steps: You already know: Ich finde das Zimmer schön (A1) and weil with the verb at the end (A2 chapter 1).
New today: set phrases for opinions (Redemittel): Ich finde, Meiner Meinung nach, dafür, dagegen, and how to agree or disagree.
By the end you can: give your opinion with a reason, ask for the opinion of others and answer them.

examples.en: I find the room nice.
examples.why: You know this: Ich finde + thing + adjective.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich müde bin.
examples.en: I stay at home because I am tired.
examples.why: You know this: the weil verb is last.

examples.de: Ich finde Schuluniformen gut, weil alle gleich aussehen.
examples.en: I find school uniforms good because everyone looks the same.
examples.why: New today: your opinion and a reason in one sentence.

cards.more: Imagine you are building with ready-made blocks instead of single bricks. A phrase like Meiner Meinung nach is one block: you take it, you put it at the start, and you add your idea. You do not need to think about every word. A reason is one more block: weil and then your reason. With three or four blocks in your pocket you can join almost any talk about school, and you sound natural at once. Today you collect these blocks.

cards.title: Strategy: learn whole phrases (Redemittel)
cards.body: Redemittel are ready-made phrases for a purpose: giving an opinion, agreeing, disagreeing. Learn them as whole pieces, not as single words. Put them in three boxes: my opinion, I agree, I disagree. When you speak, you take a piece out of the box and add your idea.

examples.en: You are right.
examples.why: Box: I agree. Learn it as one piece.

examples.en: I see it the same way.
I see it differently.

cards.lead: In the introduction you used one opinion sentence. On this card: a learning trick, Redemittel, so you speak faster and do not search for single words.

deeper.text: The trick is to learn the whole chunk and to say it aloud. Chunks are fast, because your brain already knows the order. Do not translate them word by word: Da hast du recht is simply you are right. Make three little boxes on paper and write two phrases in each box. Then use one of them in your next talk.

example.en: That is true.

cards.more: Think of a toolbox. A hammer is not made of single screws: it is one tool. Phrases like Da hast du recht are tools too. You do not build them every time. You grab them from the box, and you use them. Step 1: make three boxes. Step 2: put two phrases in each. Step 3: say each phrase aloud three times. Step 4: use a phrase in a real chat. That is the whole strategy.

rows: Meiner Meinung nach ist das gut.
In my opinion that is good.
I see it the same way.

steps: 1 Make three boxes: my opinion, I agree, I disagree.
2 Put two phrases in each box.
3 Say each phrase aloud.
4 Use one in your next talk.

cards.title: My opinion: finde, denke, Meiner Meinung nach
cards.body: Three ways to give an opinion. Ich finde + thing + adjective: Ich finde Schuluniformen gut. Ich denke, + a normal sentence: Ich denke, das ist gut. Meiner Meinung nach + verb: the phrase fills position 1, so the verb comes right after it: Meiner Meinung nach ist das gut.

examples.en: I find the hall great.
I think homework is important.
examples.why: After the comma: a normal sentence, verb in position 2.

examples.de: Meiner Meinung nach ist das gut.
examples.en: In my opinion that is good.
examples.why: The phrase is position 1, so the verb is next.

cards.lead: You have the three boxes. On this card: three set phrases for the box my opinion, and the one place where the verb must go.

deeper.text: Nach normally stands before its noun, but in meiner Meinung nach it stands behind: it is a fixed chunk. Learn it as one piece. After Ich denke, there is a comma and then a normal sentence. Nothing moves to the end. Do not put the verb of the second sentence at the end here: it is not a weil sentence.

example.de: Meiner Meinung nach sind Tests wichtig.
example.en: In my opinion tests are important.

cards.more: Opinion frames are like three picture frames. In the first frame you hang a thing and an adjective: Ich finde Schuluniformen gut. The second frame has a comma in the middle and a normal sentence behind it: Ich denke, das ist gut. The third frame is a small block in front: Meiner Meinung nach. Everything behind it follows the normal rule: the verb is next. Meiner Meinung nach ist das gut. Check the little verb after nach.

rows: Meiner Meinung nach ist das gut.

cards.title: For or against: dafür, dagegen, für, gegen
cards.body: Say Ich bin dafür for in favour and Ich bin dagegen for against. If you name the thing, use für or gegen with the accusative: Ich bin für den Test, Ich bin gegen den Test. The accusative is the one you know: den, die, das, die.

examples.en: I am in favour.
I am against the test.
Leon is for school uniforms.
examples.why: für + accusative. Plural does not change.

cards.lead: You can say what you think. On this card: how to say for and against, alone and with a thing, so you can take a side in a discussion.

deeper.text: Dafür and dagegen are tiny chunks. They already contain the thing you mean, so nothing follows: Ich bin dagegen. If you want the thing, break the chunk apart: dafür becomes für, dagegen becomes gegen, and the thing comes after, in the accusative. Gegen is a new word, but it follows the rule you know for für.

example.en: Mira is against the homework.

cards.more: Dafür and dagegen are like two buttons, green and red. Green means yes, red means no. If you press a button, you do not need to say more. If you want to say what you mean, replace the button with its small piece: für or gegen. Then the thing follows, in the accusative: für den Test, gegen den Test, für die Pause. Step 1: say the button. Step 2: add the thing if you want.

cards.title: Agree and disagree
cards.body: To agree: Das stimmt. Da hast du recht. Das sehe ich auch so. Ich stimme dir zu. To disagree: Das sehe ich anders. Nein, das stimmt nicht. Ich widerspreche dir. Zustimmen is a separable verb and, like widersprechen, it takes the dative: dir, not dich.

examples.en: I agree with you.
I disagree with you.
Anna agrees with Ben.
examples.why: The person is in the dative.

cards.lead: You can take a side. On this card: the phrases for agreeing and disagreeing, and two new verbs that always take the dative.

deeper.text: Zustimmen and widersprechen belong to the dative verb family: helfen, gehören, antworten. Whoever you agree with or contradict is in the dative: dir, mir, ihm, Ben. Zustimmen is separable, like aufstehen: Ich stimme dir zu. Widersprechen changes e to i for du and er: du widersprichst, er widerspricht.

example.en: Mira disagrees with Ben.

cards.more: Think of the two verbs as two friends in the dative club. Zustimmen means to say yes to a person. Widersprechen means to say no to a person. The person is always in the dative: dir. Ich stimme dir zu. Ich widerspreche dir. Never dich. Zustimmen also splits like aufstehen: the prefix zu goes to the end. Step 1: take the person. Step 2: put them in the dative. Step 3: send zu to the end.

cards.title: Reasons with weil, advantage and disadvantage
cards.body: Give a reason with weil: the verb goes to the end. Ich bin dafür, weil alle gleich aussehen. Use Vorteil (advantage) and Nachteil (disadvantage) to weigh both sides: Ein Vorteil ist: Alle sind gleich. After the colon you write a normal sentence. In many places in Germany there are almost no school uniforms.

examples.de: Ich bin dafür, weil alle gleich aussehen.
examples.en: I am in favour because everyone looks the same.

examples.de: Ich bin dagegen, weil ich meine Kleidung mag.
examples.en: I am against it because I like my clothes.

examples.de: Ein Vorteil ist: Alle sind gleich.
examples.en: One advantage is: everyone is the same.

cards.lead: You can agree and disagree. On this card: giving a reason with weil, and weighing advantage and disadvantage, so your opinion sounds convincing.

deeper.text: A reason is what makes an opinion strong. Without a reason, Ich bin dagegen is only a button. With weil you add the why: weil ich müde bin. The verb is last, as you know. Vorteil and Nachteil help you give both sides: first an advantage, then a disadvantage. Many speakers say: Ein Vorteil ist … und ein Nachteil ist …

example.de: Ein Nachteil ist: Ich habe keine Zeit.
example.en: One disadvantage is: I have no time.

cards.more: An opinion is like a table. The top is your opinion: Ich bin dafür. The legs are your reasons. Without legs the table falls. One leg is weil with its verb at the end. Another leg is a Vorteil: Ein Vorteil ist … The Nachteil is the other side of the table. If you know both sides, your opinion stands very firm. Say: Ich bin dafür, weil … and then: Ein Nachteil ist …

rows: Ich kann meine Kleidung nicht zeigen.

cards.title: Ask for opinions
cards.body: To ask for an opinion: Was meinst du? Wie findest du Schuluniformen? Und du, was denkst du? Answer with a frame from this lesson: Ich finde … Meiner Meinung nach … Ich bin dafür. Asking back keeps the talk alive, because both people speak.

examples.en: What do you think?
How do you find school uniforms?
And you, what do you think?
examples.why: Ask back after your own answer.

cards.lead: You can give reasons. On this card: three questions that ask for an opinion, so you can invite other people into the talk.

deeper.text: A question about an opinion has the verb in position 2, like every question with a question word: Was meinst du? Wie findest du das? The second one needs a thing: Wie findest du Schuluniformen? Und du? is the shortest way to ask back. Add a question word if you want: Und du, was denkst du?

example.en: How do you find the hall?

cards.more: A talk is like a ball game. You throw your opinion, then you throw the ball back. How? With a question: Was meinst du? Wie findest du das? Und du? The other person catches it and answers with a frame: Ich finde das gut. Meiner Meinung nach ist das gut. Then they throw it back with Und du? Step 1: give your opinion. Step 2: throw the ball with a question.

deeper.text: Good speakers use all four steps, but they keep it short. One opinion, one reason, one question. Then they listen and answer. You do not need long sentences. Listen for the small phrases: Da hast du recht, Das sehe ich anders. They are the glue of every talk. Read the dialogue aloud with a friend and swap roles.

example.en: What do you think?

cards.more: A discussion is a dance with four steps. Step 1: say what you think. Step 2: say why. Step 3: ask the other person. Step 4: agree or disagree. Mira and Ben dance it in six lines. lessons.title: Das Schulsystem: types of school, a comment and a short presentation
lessons.goal: Name the school types, compare school in the past and today, write a short forum comment and give a short talk about school.

grammar.point: School types: die Hauptschule, die Realschule, das Gymnasium, die Gesamtschule, die Berufsschule, die Hochschule. wo? takes the dative (in der Grundschule, auf dem Gymnasium), wohin? takes the accusative (in die Grundschule, auf das Gymnasium). Compare old and new with man + past and present modals: Früher musste man …, heute muss man … A comment has four steps (greeting, opinion, reason, closing).
grammar.oneLine: Ich gehe auf das Gymnasium. Ich war auf dem Gymnasium. Wohin? accusative, wo? dative.

mistake.why: Gehen is a movement, so you ask wohin? and use the accusative: das Gymnasium. Auf dem Gymnasium only says where you are.

terms.meaning: a general you or one: people in general. It takes the verb ending of er/sie/es
the rule that children must go to school
ready-made phrases for a purpose, such as giving an opinion
a short text you write online to give your opinion

cards.title: Before we start: school in three countries
cards.body: Wie ist die Schule in Deutschland, in Österreich und in der Schweiz? When you meet people from other countries, you often talk about school. Today you learn the school types and you practise everything from this chapter: wo or wohin, past and present, opinion and reason.
steps: You already know: In Deutschland geht man mit sechs in die Schule. You also know the articles in three cases and the set phrases for opinions.
New today: the school types after primary school, the school systems of Germany, Austria and Switzerland, a comment and a short talk.
By the end you can: write a short comment and give a short talk about school.

examples.de: In Deutschland geht man mit sechs in die Schule.
examples.en: In Germany you go to school at six.

examples.de: Nach der Grundschule gibt es viele Schulen.
examples.en: After primary school there are many schools.
examples.why: New today: es gibt means there is or there are. It is a chunk.

cards.more: Imagine a map with roads. After primary school the road splits into several roads: Hauptschule, Realschule, Gymnasium, Gesamtschule. Each road leads somewhere else, but all of them can lead to a good job. Today you learn the names of the roads and how to say where you go and where you are. Then you use all your set phrases to write and speak about it.

cards.title: The school types in Germany
cards.body: After the Grundschule there are several kinds of school: die Hauptschule, die Realschule, das Gymnasium, die Gesamtschule. After that, many people go to die Berufsschule for an Ausbildung, or to die Hochschule after the Abitur. In many places the names are a little different. Es gibt means there is or there are: learn it as a chunk.

examples.de: In Deutschland gibt es die Hauptschule.
examples.en: In Germany there is the Hauptschule.
examples.why: es gibt: a chunk. The thing that exists is the accusative.

examples.de: Nach dem Abitur besucht man die Hochschule.
examples.en: After the Abitur you go to a university.
examples.why: After mit and nach: the dative.

examples.de: Ben möchte in die Berufsschule gehen.
examples.en: Ben wants to go to the vocational school.

cards.lead: In the introduction you saw the road split after primary school. On this card: the school types and their articles, so you can name the roads people take.

deeper.text: These names are not the same everywhere, because the states of Germany decide. In many places the Hauptschule and the Realschule have joined or have other names. So listen for the words and ask: Wie heißt die Schule bei euch? The articles stay: die Hauptschule, die Realschule, das Gymnasium, die Gesamtschule. Learn the article together with the noun.

example.de: Die Gesamtschule ist eine Schule für alle.
example.en: The Gesamtschule is a school for everyone.

cards.more: Picture a road with a fork. Step 1: everybody walks the Grundschule road. Step 2: the road splits: Hauptschule, Realschule, Gymnasium or Gesamtschule. Step 3: after that, some people go to the Berufsschule for a job training, and others go to the Hochschule after the Abitur. You do not need to know all the details: just learn the six names with their articles, and how to say where you go.

cards.title: wo? or wohin? with school types
cards.body: The same rule as in lesson 7. Wo? is dative: in der Grundschule, auf dem Gymnasium. Wohin? is accusative: in die Grundschule, auf das Gymnasium. The small word often depends on the school: in with Grundschule, Realschule and Berufsschule, auf with Gymnasium, an with Hochschule. Learn each one as a chunk.

examples.en: I was in primary school.
Leon was at the Gymnasium.

examples.de: Mit zehn gehen viele Kinder auf das Gymnasium.
examples.en: At ten many children go to the Gymnasium.

cards.lead: You know the school types. On this card: wo? and wohin? with them, so you can say which school you were in and which one you go to.

deeper.text: In English you say at school, to school, at university. In German the small word changes with the school type, so learn it with the noun. Be careful with the verb: war or bin tells you wo?, gehen tells you wohin?. A common mistake is Ich gehe auf dem Gymnasium: gehen is a movement, so you need auf das.

example.en: I was at the Realschule.

cards.more: Same door as before. Inside the school: wo? dative, in der Grundschule. Walking into the school: wohin? accusative, in die Grundschule. The only new thing is the small word: in, auf or an. Step 1: say the school type. Step 2: pick the small word you learned with it. Step 3: stay or move? Dative or accusative. Step 4: read the table. If you are not sure, ask a friend: Sagt man in der Realschule or auf der Realschule? Both exist.

cards.title: Austria and Switzerland in two lines
cards.body: In Austria and in Switzerland school looks similar, but the names differ. At the end of the Gymnasium you take the Matura, in Germany the Abitur. In all three countries there is a Schulpflicht: children must go to school. A Kindergarten comes first, and many places have a Ganztagsschule, a school with lessons in the afternoon.

examples.de: In Deutschland gibt es das Abitur.
examples.en: In Germany there is the Abitur.

examples.de: In Österreich und in der Schweiz gibt es die Matura.
examples.en: In Austria and in Switzerland there is the Matura.

examples.de: Viele Kinder gehen in den Kindergarten.
examples.en: Many children go to the kindergarten.

cards.lead: You can name the school types. On this card: a small table about Germany, Austria and Switzerland, and the words Schulpflicht, Kindergarten and Ganztagsschule, so you can compare school in different countries.

deeper.text: These facts are general: they change from state to state or canton to canton. In Switzerland the cantons decide, in Germany the states do. Ask a person from the country, and listen for the words. In every country the Schulpflicht means the same: children must go to school for a number of years.

example.de: Die Schulpflicht beginnt mit sechs Jahren.
example.en: Compulsory schooling begins at six years old.

cards.more: Imagine a small table with three columns: country, who decides, exam at the end. Germany, Austria and Switzerland all have a Schulpflicht. The final exam has a different name: Abitur in Germany, Matura in Austria and Switzerland. Before school there is the Kindergarten, and after lunch some schools still have lessons: that is the Ganztagsschule. Step 1: read the table. Step 2: say one fact about each country.

cards.title: Past and present with man
cards.body: To compare old and new, use man with a modal: Früher musste man eine Schuluniform tragen. Heute muss man keine Schuluniform tragen. The past modals (musste, durfte, konnte) and the present modals (muss, darf, kann) both keep the second verb at the end.

examples.de: Früher musste man eine Schuluniform tragen.
examples.en: Back then you had to wear a school uniform.

examples.de: Heute darf man ein Handy mitbringen.
examples.en: Today you may bring a phone.

examples.de: Heute kann man im Computerraum arbeiten.
examples.en: Today you can work in the computer room.

cards.lead: You know the school types. On this card: man with past and present modals, so you can say how school was and how it is today.

deeper.text: Man is a general you: it means people in general. It takes the verb ending of er/sie/es: man muss, man darf, man kann. In the past the same: man musste, man durfte, man konnte. Use früher and heute as a pair to show the change. Keep in mind: the second verb waits at the end.

example.de: Früher konnte man nur in der Klasse lernen.
example.en: Back then you could only study in the class.

cards.more: A comparison needs two pictures: before and now. Step 1: say früher. Step 2: use a past modal: musste, durfte, konnte. Step 3: say the thing, and put the second verb at the end. Step 4: say heute and use the present modal: muss, darf, kann. The two sentences look the same, only the modal and the time word change. Say them in pairs, like a see-saw: früher, heute.

Heute muss man keine Schuluniform tragen.
Früher durfte man kein Handy mitbringen.
Heute darf man ein Handy mitbringen.
Früher konnte man nur in der Klasse lernen.
Heute kann man im Computerraum lernen.

2 Use a past modal: musste, durfte, konnte.
3 Put the second verb at the end.
4 Say heute and use the present modal.

cards.title: Writing a comment in an online forum
cards.body: A short comment has four steps. 1 Greeting: Hallo! 2 Opinion: Meiner Meinung nach sind Schuluniformen gut. 3 Reason: Ich bin dafür, weil alle gleich aussehen. 4 Closing: Viele Grüße or Liebe Grüße, and your name. Learn Viele Grüße and Liebe Grüße as whole chunks.

examples.de: Meiner Meinung nach sind Schuluniformen gut.
examples.en: In my opinion school uniforms are good.
examples.why: Step 2: opinion with the verb right after nach.

examples.de: Ich bin gegen Schuluniformen, weil ich meine Kleidung mag.
examples.en: I am against school uniforms because I like my clothes.
examples.why: Step 3: reason with weil, the verb is last.

examples.en: Best wishes from Mira

cards.lead: You can compare past and present. On this card: a four-step model for a short online comment, so you know what to write and in which order.

deeper.text: A good comment is short and clear. One opinion, one reason, a friendly start and end. In a forum people write Hallo! at the start, and they close with Viele Grüße or Liebe Grüße. Viele Grüße is a little more neutral, Liebe Grüße is warmer. Do not forget the comma after the closing chunk and write your name on the next line.

example.en: Kind regards from Ben

cards.more: A comment is a sandwich with four layers. Top bread: Hallo! First layer: your opinion with Meiner Meinung nach. Second layer: your reason with weil. Bottom bread: Viele Grüße and your name. If you have these four layers, your comment is complete. Step 1: Hallo! Step 2: opinion. Step 3: reason. Step 4: closing. Then read it once aloud to check the verb at the end of the weil part.

rows: Meiner Meinung nach sind Schuluniformen gut.
Ich bin dafür, weil alle gleich aussehen.

steps: 1 Greeting: Hallo!
2 Opinion: Meiner Meinung nach …
3 Reason: … weil …
4 Closing: Viele Grüße and your name.

cards.title: A short talk about school
cards.body: A short talk has five steps. 1 Say the topic: Ich möchte über die Schule in Österreich sprechen. 2 Say what exists: In Österreich gibt es … 3 Say how it was: Früher musste man … 4 Say your opinion: Meiner Meinung nach … 5 Say thanks: Vielen Dank! Use the phrases from lesson 8.

examples.en: I would like to talk about school in Austria.
examples.why: Step 1: topic. Learn the whole chunk.

examples.en: Back then you had to study a lot.
Thank you very much!

cards.lead: You can write a comment. On this card: a five-step plan for a short talk, so you can speak about school without getting lost.

deeper.text: A talk is easier when you know the plan. Write one sentence for each step on a card. Then you can speak with the card in your hand. Ich möchte über … sprechen is a chunk: you only change the topic. Stay short: five sentences are enough. Speak slowly and look at your listeners.

example.de: Meiner Meinung nach ist das gut.
example.en: In my opinion that is good.

cards.more: A talk is like a staircase with five steps. Step 1: say what you talk about. Step 2: say what exists. Step 3: say how it was before. Step 4: say what you think. Step 5: say thanks. At each step you put one foot down: one sentence. After five steps you are at the top. You can write the five sentences on a small card, one line each. That is your whole talk.

In Österreich gibt es die Matura.
Meiner Meinung nach ist das gut.

steps: 1 Say the topic.

4 Say your opinion.
5 Say thanks.

cards.title: Read a school-system text
cards.body: Now you read a short text about school in Germany. Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again and underline the verbs. The table shows the text line by line. Use the glossary in your head: die Berufsschule is the vocational school, die Hochschule is the university.

cards.lead: This is the last card. On this card: a short text that uses everything from the lesson, so you practise reading about school and finding the verbs.

deeper.text: To read well, do not translate every word. First find the verbs: they tell you who does what. Then find the nouns: they tell you the topic. If a word is new, guess from the other words around it. The words you already know are many: Grundschule, Gymnasium, Abitur, Ausbildung. The text is only 60 words, so you can read it twice in one minute.

example.en: After that there are many schools.

Step 2: underline the verbs, one per sentence. Step 3: look at the nouns next to them. Step 4: say in your own words what the text is about. With the table you can do the job line by line, and the last column shows you the verb.

reading.title: Mira erzählt: Meine Schulzeit
reading.text: Ich war Schülerin in Hamburg. Früher musste ich um sechs Uhr aufstehen, weil mein Schulweg lang war. Ich wollte immer auf dem Schulhof spielen, aber ich musste zuerst die Hausaufgaben machen. In Mathe konnte ich gut rechnen, und ich mochte Kunst. Aber ich konnte nicht malen! Unsere Lehrerin war streng. Wir durften im Unterricht nicht essen, und wir sollten immer leise sein. Nachmittags wollte ich spielen, aber ich sollte lernen. Ich konnte schon früh Gitarre spielen, und das war toll. Unsere Lehrerin hat mich oft gelobt. Mein Lieblingsfach war Geschichte. In der Pause hatte ich oft Hunger, weil ich morgens nicht essen konnte.

reading.text: Ich heiße Ben. In der Grundschule war ich gern in der Klasse. Ich habe das Abitur gemacht, und ich bin nie sitzengeblieben. Nach der Schule wollte ich nicht studieren. In den Ferien habe ich einen Ferienjob im Restaurant gemacht. Der Chef war Herr Ali. Das war toll! Mein Bruder hat auch einen Ferienjob gemacht, und wir haben oft zusammen gearbeitet. Ich habe mit meinem Chef gesprochen, und er hat mir viel gezeigt. Danach habe ich bei meiner Tante in Wien gewohnt und eine Lehre als Koch gemacht. Vor einem Jahr habe ich die Lehre abgeschlossen. reading.text:
Hallo! Wir sind die Klasse 8b, und das ist unser Schulprojekt. Anna schreibt den Text, und Frau Weber ist unsere Lehrerin. Unsere Schule hat einen Computerraum, eine Aula, eine Schwimmhalle und einen Sportplatz. Am Schwarzen Brett steht ein Zettel: Heute um vier Uhr ist ein Treffen in der Aula. Früher durften wir nicht auf den Sportplatz gehen. Jetzt dürfen wir dort spielen. Früher musste man eine Schuluniform tragen. Wir waren dagegen, weil wir unsere Kleidung mögen. Heute muss man keine Schuluniform tragen. Der Schulbus fährt um sieben Uhr. Der Fahrradständer ist neben dem Eingang. Wir haben auch ein Labor. Wie findest du unsere Schule? Viele Grüße
Anna
